Hon. Warren Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East) moved:
That this House condemn the Government for its failure to initiate meaningful reform in the unemployment insurance system and for its failure to commit itself to a full employment policy that seriously addresses high regional unemployment, youth unemployment, part-time work and labour market adjustment.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the resolution before the House today deals with two important issues which are intimately related to each other. First, it deals with the important issue of unemployment and the need for full employment policies which should be our first and highest priority. It then deals with unemployment insurance policies which are essential for those who are put out of work, contrary to their will. I will deal first with the question of unemployment insurance.
On Friday, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) told the House that because the Government could not make up its mind it would do nothing with respect to the reform of the Unemployment Insurance Act.
In November, 1984, when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) made his famous financial statement, he said that unemployment insurance reform was one of the priorities of the Government. In his booklet entitled A New Direction for Canada: An Agenda for Economic Renewal, he set out some of the problems that were being experienced with unemployment insurance and also listed some questions that he wanted answered. At that time in November, 1984, he said this was an urgent matter. However, it took the Government until 1985 to set up the Forget Commission which consisted of five persons and eventually cost approximately $7 million.
The House should also note that just prior to the appointment of the Forget Commission there was also the Macdonald Royal Commission on Economic Prospects which studied the issue of unemployment insurance as well as the problems of unemployment, and the Newfoundland Royal Commission on Unemployment. In that period from 1985 to 1987, three Royal Commissions looked at this important subject.
May 19, 1987

The Forget Commission reported in December, 1986, with 53 recommendations. The recommendations which received the most attention, because they were the most controversial, were those relating to its annualization proposal and its proposals to cut extended regional benefits and fishermen's benefits. The annualization proposal was one for a new method of calculating unemployment insurance benefits and, according to which, there would have been serious cuts in benefits for people who were plagued with seasonal unemployment, parttime work, and the like.
While recommending this new annualization scheme which would have cut benefits, and recommending the removal of the extended regional benefits and fishermen's benefits, Mr. Forget also made a vague recommendation that new programs be set up for a guaranteed income and for regional development. However, he did not give any detail.
The recommendations in his report would have amounted to S3 billion in cuts in a $12 billion program. Those cuts would have had a particular impact on Atlantic Canada, the east and north of Quebec, the north of Ontario, and in the north of our western provinces, including most of British Columbia and Alberta.
Workers in Canada might have been willing to consider a package of proposals whereby there would have been cuts in the unemployment insurance system due to some inconsistency with the principles of unemployment insurance if Mr. Forget had also tabled a detailed plan for regional economic expansion and development and for a new guaranteed income program. Without such details, however, no worker in this country who has been chronically hit by unemployment will give up a good program, which they know, even if imperfect, for vague, pie-in-the-sky proposals related to guaranteed income and regional development.
On Friday the Minister could have recognized that deficiency in the Forget Commission recommendations, rather than copping out entirely on unemployment insurance reform.
When the standing committee studied the Forget Report, even members of the Forget Commission told us that they understood why Canadians would not be willing to accept their proposal on annualization and the cutting of regional benefits and fishermen's benefits without seeing the details of a replacement program. They said they understood that.
The Minister could have come to the House on Friday and, instead of saying there would be no reform whatsoever in this field, said those proposals of Mr. Forget or similar ones would be put on the back burner while the Government was preparing, as suggested by Mr. Forget, new programs for regional economic expansion and for income support. But the whole subject is forgotten altogether.
Immediately after the tabling of the Forget Report the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration took notice of the report and undertook a study of the
Supply
same issues. It looked at the recommendations made by Forget and at the alternatives which had been discussed in the country, and heard witnesses. As a member of the standing committee I thought that in a short period of time we did a good job in studying the principal issues. We came out with a report in March, just a few months ago, in which we made 90 recommendations for reform. There was unanimous agreement in the committee on 89 of the recommendations. In other words, the Conservative, New Democrat and Liberal Members of the committee agreed that we could and should move ahead with reform of the unemployment insurance system, and we agreed unanimously on 89 recommendations.
If we compare the 90 recommendations with the 53 recommendations in the Forget Report, we find there is a lot of common ground. It is true, as I mentioned a few moments ago, there was a lot of controversy with respect to the Forget recommendations relating to annualization, regional benefits and fishermen's benefits. However, there were other recommendations in respect of which there was less controversy because they were well accepted throughout the country. The standing committee took those recommendations and I think improved on them.
I might just mention some of those recommendations relating to serious deficiencies in the unemployment insurance system, and where there was agreement between Forget and the standing committee, and where the Minister could have taken action.
To begin with, with respect to the whole area of training, it has been a bit of a scandal that in the past an individual was not able to go on a training program he or she had chosen if receiving unemployment insurance, because the basic rules of unemployment insurance require that one must always be ready and available for work.
A few years ago, under the previous Liberal Government, certain amendments were made so that a person collecting unemployment insurance could take certain specified training programs, and we had a certain experience with that, but it was not good enough.
Both the Forget Commission and the standing committee recommended that a person receiving unemployment insurance should be able to participate in a wide range of training programs precisely because if we want this person to go back into the labour market fully employed, and he is an untrained person, the only way he is going to get full-time employment or reasonable employment is by becoming trained. Although, as I said, when putting together the unemployment insurance program we had established a principle that one must be ready and available for work, how silly it is to use that principle to prevent someone from getting training which would give him or her a meaningful chance at employment.
The standing committee made recommendations about that, as did Forget, but those recommendations have been set aside. Both Forget and the standing committee made recommendations to extend unemployment insurance into the area of part-

May 19, 1987
Supply
time work. This would have meant that those who are in parttime work would pay contributions in proportion to their incomes and receive benefits in proportion to their incomes.
As you probably know, Mr. Speaker, there are many individuals doing part-time work. About 71 per cent of them are women. They are working part time in order to supplement the incomes of their spouse. That additional income is very important in supporting the family. Some of these women are in part-time jobs for two, three and four years and their earnings become extremely important as part of the family income. If that person is laid off, the family is in serious difficulty. There is no reason why people in part-time work should not receive unemployment insurance. That was recognized by Forget and it was recognized by the standing committee.
Another situation about which there is a lot of concern in Canada is when overpayments are made to individuals under the Unemployment Insurance Act and, after the overpayment is discovered, a claim is made against that person to reimburse the amount of overpayment. We can understand a demand for return of overpayment if the overpayment was the fault of the claimant. However, in many cases the fault for the overpayment rests with officials in the Unemployment Insurance Commission. Sometimes there are horrendous situations where people who are still unemployed, or who have gone beyond unemployment and are on social welfare, are asked to pay back sums of money they cannot afford. It is true the Unemployment Insurance Commission will make arrangements with these people, but there is the whole principle of harassing these people for overpayments for which they were not responsible.
Just recently there was an article in The Globe and Mail reporting on a problem in Quebec which was raised by a Conservative Member. Eighteen women in a Gaspe village were being asked to repay up to $13,000 each for overpayments that were made to them, not because of their fault but because of the fault of officials. The Hon. Member from Gaspe went to bat for them but, unfortunately, the matter has not been resolved satisfactorily. In any case, the standing committee made recommendations to deal with this problem. It is again unfortunate that we could not make reforms in those areas.
With respect to maternity and parental benefits, again there was common ground between the standing committee and the Forget Commission in taking action in this area, particularly to eliminate the two-week waiting period in the case of maternity benefits. A birth is something which happens in the natural course of events. It is not planned deliberately in the sense that one cannot pick the date. There was agreement there but again there was no action taken.
Another problem which has lingered on for the last few years which requires reform arises in the situation where workers in a plant who are not on strike are locked out when another union in the same plant goes on strike. We all agree that if one deliberately goes on strike one has no right to unemployment insurance benefits. However, there must be
clarification with respect to those workers who have been locked out due to a strike in which they are not involved, or they cannot cross picket lines. Again, the Forget Commission and the standing committee made recommendations to correct that situation.
Finally, the standing committee and the Forget Commission made recommendations to restructure the Unemployment Insurance Commission so that it would have better representation from both workers and employers; it would be more independent and efficient. Again, this is an area where the Minister could have acted and he did not.
While these issues are all critical to many thousands of Canadians, they are not controversial in the way in which the issues of annualization and severe cuts were. I might say that the standing committee in hearing evidence on these matters heard from trade unions and others that workers would be willing to pay increases in their contributions if they were able to get improved benefits.
As I stated earlier, these reforms could have been implemented pending a more profound reform of the unemployment insurance system coupled with a new income support system and a new regional development program. But, no, the Government has decided to do nothing. It abdicated its responsibility. It took the path of least resistance. And all this after a $7 million study conducted by Forget, not to mention the work carried out by the Macdonald Royal Commission, the Newfoundland Royal Commission and the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration.
Unemployment insurance was introduced in 1940 after the tragedies of the 1930s, the Great Depression of 1929 and the massive unemployment that followed. Unemployment Insurance was a great Liberal accomplishment. But we Liberals have always agreed that reform is necessary. As a matter of fact, over the years Bills have been brought in to reform and update the Unemployment Insurance Act. We still favour fine-tuning and reforming of the Act.
Unemployment insurance is not only good for those workers who are unemployed but it is good for the country. It is good for business. If we look at the phenomenon that took place in the Great Depression of the 1930s when there was no unemployment insurance, we see that as men and women were laid off they lost their purchasing power. The phenomenon hit businesses in the community sooner or later. It hit the corner stores. Mortgages were foreclosed. People could not pay their rents. There was a snowball effect that took place which went well beyond the original numbers of people who were laid off. So unemployment insurance, to the extent that it maintains purchasing power when times are bad, is good for the whole community and also good for business.
There are those people in the country, and their names are listed as witnesses who appeared before the standing committee and the Forget Commission, who complained that we must
May 19, 1987

make massive cuts in the unemployment insurance system because there are so many cheaters. Forget himself found that cheaters on unemployment insurance amount to less than 3 per cent of the total claimants in a program which amounts to approximately $12 billion. As a matter of fact, there are fewer cheaters on unemployment insurance than there are in terms of income tax.
In his statement on Friday, the Minister of Employment and Immigration also said that his first priority would be to create employment so that people would not have to make claims on unemployment insurance. We all applaud that statement of principle. Unfortunately, the Minister did not go on to give any evidence of new programs or a new commitment to deal with the unemployment problem. It appears that this is just more of the politics of rhetoric.
Since 1984, budgets for employment creation and training have been cut by 30 per cent. Budgets in this area totalled $2.2 billion in 1984. They have now been reduced to $1.6 billion. There have also been cuts in budgets for regional economic development. This morning we read that the entire Department may be done away with. The Government is going to get out of regional development altogether.
It is true that the rate of unemployment has been brought down from about 12.5 per cent in 1983 to 9.3 per cent in the most recent months.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-UI REFORM-FULL EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-UI REFORM-FULL EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
The Minister applauds. Three years after the recession he is applauding a 9.3 per cent unemployment rate.
In 1981, the year before the recession, the rate of unemployment was 7.5 per cent. It jumped up to over 11 per cent in one year due to world-wide economic conditions. The fact is that during the period of time under Liberal Governments from 1965 to 1980 the average rate of unemployment was 5.6 per cent. We were a Government that cared about the unemployed.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-UI REFORM-FULL EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-UI REFORM-FULL EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Here we are three years out of the recession and the rate of unemployment is still 9.3 per cent as a result of the Government's reliance on a laissez-faire approach to unemployment. The Government still takes great joy in the fact that we have a rate of unemployment of 9.3 per cent.
Members of the Government repeat over and over again the number of jobs that have been created. But in a report which came out in February of this year we were told that more than 95 per cent of the new jobs created last year were created in one province, that is, in the Province of Ontario. Some 95 per cent of the new jobs created last year were created in Ontario, and most of them were created in southern Ontario. It must be pointed out to the Government that in Ontario we have a Liberal Government which is at least trying to do something about the situation.
Supply
More than 40 per cent of the 11.6 million jobs in Canada are located in the economic heartland of Canada where 36 per cent of the total population lives. This morning there was a report from the Conference Board of Canada which states that while there may be improvement again next year in Ontario and Quebec, the unemployment rate will climb in all the other provinces.
If we take Ontario out of the picture-and Ontario is an important place and we are all pleased to see things going so well in southern Ontario-we note that Ontario is not Canada. If we rely simply on a market economy approach, a laissez-faire approach, we will end up with a situation in which one part of the country does enormously well while the other part does poorly. That is not acceptable in Canada. It has never been acceptable in Canada.
Despite the challenges, governments of the country, and I might say former Conservative Governments, have tried to do something about regional economic problems, but the present Government has abdicated its role in this area. It seems that it will abdicate it still more.
In addition to the unfair distribution of job creation and the unfair distribution of economic growth we also have a great increase in part-time jobs in terms of recovery in employment. People who were working formerly in highly paid industrial jobs have been cut out of those jobs and are now going back into the job market in lower paying service jobs. Part-time work in Canada increased 73 per cent from 1976 to 1986 while full-time work has increased by only 17 per cent. In 1976, only 11 per cent of those in part-time work did not want to work part-time. Today, 30 per cent are dissatisfied with employment in part-time work.
As I mentioned earlier, 75 per cent of those in part-time work are women. Their wage gap started to widen this year for the first time in 18 years. It is all part of the same picture, this increase in part-time work, more women into part-time work, and their wage gap beginning to widen.
Again, the Government speaks about its wish to do something about high unemployment and problems in the employment field, but it puts forward no new programs. The response of the Government to all of these problems-the high rates of regional unemployment, the high rates of part-time work, the growing gap between the rich and the poor and the growing gap between the wages of men and women-is rhetoric and political flimflam.
The Government has said over and over again that things are better than they were in 1983. That is no great accomplishment. The Government would have something to brag about if it could bring the rate of unemployment down to what it was in pre-recession times, to at least 7.5 per cent or the average of 5.6 per cent that it was in the 1960s and 1970s.
The reason we are left with this situation is that the Government has an extremely laissez-faire approach to it. Liberal Governments have always believed in the free enterprise system, but we also believe that there is a strong role to

May 19, 1987
Supply
be played by Government. Where there are problems in the regions and where there are problems with key groups of unemployed we should do something about them. The greatest levels of prosperity in this country have come when we have had the proper mix of public and private expenditure with respect to employment. When the two have worked together, that is when we have had prosperity. We are not having prosperity now, except perhaps in the greater Toronto region.
According to a Gallup poll taken in February of this year, only a couple of months ago, 41 per cent of Canadians consider unemployment to be the greatest problem in this country. Canadians want action. They know that things can be done to improve the unemployment situation.
Twice since World War II, Liberal governments made a commitment to full employment, and twice it was achieved. After World War II, the governments of Mackenzie King and St. Laurent, following the first White Paper on Full Employment, made a commitment to full employment, and for seven years we had average unemployment in this country of 3 per cent. After returning to power in 1963, the Pearson Government, following the establishment of the Canada Economic Council, again made a commitment to full employment, and we averaged around 3.7 per cent unemployment for four years. That is what can be done, Mr. Speaker, when a commitment to full employment is made; when decreasing the unemployment level becomes the highest priority.
Many things can be done in dealing with this situation, if the Government has the political will. One is to increase the commitment to regional economic development and not to cut it back. Another is to stimulate the slow-growth areas of the country. Another is to maintain or increase purchasing power during periods of economic slow-down and not cut it back, and another is to provide the essential economic infrastructure that is required in this country in order for private business to do its job properly.
The proper economic infrastructure, coupled with a serious commitment to education, training, retraining, upgrading, and research and development, can do a lot to maintain and attract employment.
In conclusion, let me say this. The Government on Friday abdicated its responsibility with respect to the reform of the unemployment insurance system. It said nothing. It just copped out completely on the subject. Some non-controversial measures could have been implemented measures that would have been helpful to many thousands of Canadians, but those measures were not taken. The Government made some brave statements with respect to dealing with the unemployed, but it announced no new programs, in fact it is cutting back while it is talking big.

Once again, Mr. Speaker, the Government has abandoned the Canadian people. Last Friday, the Minister decided to
make no changes in the unemployment insurance system but promised some major programs or measures for the unemployed in this country. Unfortunately, nothing was put on the table, not a single program, and this at a time when we have had 30 per cent cuts in job creation and training programs.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-UI REFORM-FULL EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Shame!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-UI REFORM-FULL EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
The resolution before the House, Mr. Speaker, asks this House to condemn the Government for its lack of action. But better still, I would be willing to applaud the Minister were he to stand up in his place once I have finished my remarks and say that, despite what he said on Friday last, he does have in mind certain reforms for the unemployment insurance program, that he does have in mind some new programs to help the unemployed in this country

the unemployed in the Atlantic part of the country, the unemployed in Alberta, the unemployed in British Columbia, the unemployed in eastern Quebec and northern Ontario.
If he does that, Mr. Speaker, I would be pleased to withdraw my motion and applaud the Minister.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext: Questions or comments. The Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap).

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-UI REFORM-FULL EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to commend the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand) for his motion, and also for his speech, a speech in which he covered a great many important subjects.
Without encroaching on his own time, I should like to put two questions to him. He referred to part-time work. I would ask him to expand on that, in terms of the conditions that lead to people being compelled to accept part-time work.
As well, I would ask him to expand on the conditions accounting for the high level of youth unemployment and what remedies he feels can be applied to youth unemployment.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-UI REFORM-FULL EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
I thank the Hon. Member for his questions. With respect to part-time work, a sinister phenomenon has been taking place in Canada over the last number of years in that certain large firms are deliberately laying off their fulltime staff and hiring back greater numbers of part-time workers. By doing that, these firms cut the cost of both their benefits package and the wage package. Those working fewer than 15 hours per week are not eligible for unemployment insurance, and are very often not eligible for training programs or pension programs. Often, they draw the minimum wage and are not subject to unionization. In any event, it is a more difficult matter to unionize part-time workers.
Having seen that phenomenon and its effects, the previous Government appointed the Wallace Royal Commission. That commission recommended that benefits be paid pro rata to part-time workers, thereby discouraging the movement by some firms from a full-time work-force to a part-time work-
May 19, 1987

force. Under the recommendations of the Wallace Commission, the firm would still have to pay the benefits on a pro rata basis.
While it suits the purposes of some to work part time, that is certainly not true of all. A good many people are forced to take part-time work simply because there is no full-time work available. The average part-time work week amounts to 14.5 hours, which is just under the 15 hours required to qualify for unemployment insurance eligibility.
Let me now turn to the youth unemployment problem. The major difficulty is that our young people do not have experience. Those seeking employment after high school, or even after acquiring a general arts degree or general sciences degree from university, are told by prospective employers that they do not have the experience required. The reaction of prospective employers is, I do need somebody, but I need somebody with experience.
Over and over again what we have been told by the commissions and experts is that what is needed in this country are better bridging programs, programs which will assist young people in bridging the shift from the school place to the workplace, programs which would combine training and education. It is for that reason that co-operative education programs are becoming more popular; it is for that reason that new apprenticeship programs are being promoted.
The Liberal Party, during the last election campaign, put forward the First Chance Program, a program that would have spent $1 billion putting 100,000 young people into a bridging program, thus providing them with work experience.
This Government does have some youth employment programs in place, and some bridging programs. They are not bad programs, but they deserve a bigger commitment of resources and money. They cover too few people. They are not that bad in themselves, but they do require a much greater commitment, a much greater show of political will on this Government's part.

Mr. Speaker, that is another area where there was common ground between the Forget Commission and the standing committee report. Forget recommended that those measures to cut unemployment insurance for those on preretirement pension be completely rescinded. But the Government did not do that. After a lot of starts and stops, finally the Government produced Bill C-50, which would rescind the cuts for those who applied for unemployment insurance benefits before January 5, 1986, but not for those who applied after

January 5, 1986. The Bill suggests a system which is grossly unfair. The Minister wants us to accept a Bill, one part of which is good and one part of which is terrible. We are not ready to do that quickly.
Despite that, the Minister has not once called the Bill for debate since its tabling in the House. I hear that in certain parts of the country he is blaming the delay on the Liberal and NDP opposition. As I pointed out, in a country like Canada it will not take care of everything. We are a broad, vast country with 25 million people spread all over. If we leave everything to the market-place, we will have situations just like the ones I described where 85 per cent of the new jobs go to the greater Toronto region and growing unemployment takes place in the Atlantic region and in other remote regions of the country.
One must recall that Canada has regions which are based upon one or two industries, either lumber, fisheries, agriculture, or tourism. They are subject to severe seasonal fluctuations in employment.
Since the Second World War, Governments of all stripes in Canada have taken the position that Government must intervene to redress imbalances. That is why the Department of Regional Economic Expansion and the Department of Manpower and Immigration were set up under Prime Minister Trudeau. We believe that if we left things to work themselves out they would not be worked out. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the chance today to speak for the New Democratic Party in this debate on the Government's policies on unemployment insurance and full employment.
However, first I wish to let an unemployed worker from Spadina speak to the same question. In a letter I received just recently he says in part:
The reason for this letter is simple. 1 am twenty-four years old and unemployed. I have a good education, I am willing to do most types of work, I am in good health, and I live in Toronto which has a relatively low rate of unemployment. Yet I simply cannot find a job.
I wonder if the Conservative party members really know what it is like to have no future to look forward to? I question whether the Prime Minister really cares about the thousands of people like myself. I sometimes feel that the country as a whole does not really care about the country's youth, after all we are only its future.
Farther down he says he feels that politicians must be made aware that there are thousands of people in Canada who are young, eager, and obsolete. He is far from the only one who experiences that although he says it with perhaps more eloquence than some people are able to muster in a letter.
I commend the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace- Lachine East (Mr. Allmand) for moving this motion against the background of government failure. It demands reform of the unemployment insurance system, the meeting of direct needs, including reform of unemployment insurance, social legislation, upgrading of transportation and urban infrastructure. He also refers to youth unemployment and part-time workers.
I wish to respond to three main points. First, something on which the Hon. Member has spent a great deal of time not only in his speech but in previous years as chairman of that committee, reform of the unemployment insurance system. Second, I wish to deal with the meeting of direct needs of the people, including social legislation, upgrading of transportation and urban infrastructure, and democratization of defence. Third, local control, so far as possible of production of agriculture and manufacturing products, especially for the domestic market.
On the first point, the basic principle of full employment, we must begin by declaring that full employment is not only desirable, it is essential to our people's health and happiness, as well as being economically possible and socially workable. Today we have many voices, some academic, some popular writers, and some politicians telling us that full employment is a dream, a thing of the past. They say modern technology and population growth doom us to a larger and larger share of unemployment for the work-force or, as a last resort, a fawning on the rich for personal service jobs. I say that is nonsense. In
Supply
this, one of the world's richest lands, the population has doubled since I was a youth and we are stronger and wealthier than we were then. Many here can recall, as I can, how in 1945 we returned from the Armed Forces bitterly remembering the misery and unemployment of the Dirty Thirties. We demanded full employment above all and we got it. For five years at least unemployment did not rise above 3 per cent. I firmly believe that what we did in the late 1940s we can do in the late 1980s.
However, there is one big difference. In 1945 North America had a near monopoly with the only industrial economy not wrecked by war, including the basis of industrialized agriculture. We seized the chance to dominate world markets for the export of manufactured and agricultural products and so, along with the U.S., we enjoyed three decades of easy growth. However, that is no more. Europe, the U.S.S.R. and Japan have renewed their industry and industrialized their agriculture. Brazil, India, China and other countries are rapidly industrializing. We are no longer like a man selling water in the desert. We can no longer expand our exports limitlessly. We must now rely more on our domestic market. That means we must not only ask the Canadian people what goods and services they need but also how Canadians are prepared to change our working relations and expectations and attitudes in production; how we will work together to produce these things so as to provide a market for goods and services we produce. That is the first point, the general principle of full employment, which is possible and necessary.
Second, as a foundation, we must recommit our country's resources to meeting the direct needs of the Canadian people individually and socially. The first example, of course, which we have just been considering is the unemployment insurance system which needs to be reformed. Reforms have been unanimously recommended by an all-Party committee of Parliament, predominantly a Conservative committee. They propose to include 50 weeks of benefits for 10 weeks of eligibility, coverage for part-time and short-time workers, pensions and vacations and severance pay not to be treated as earned income so as to reduce unemployment insurance benefits, maternity benefits available consecutively with regular benefits up to 50 weeks, unemployment insurance benefits funded out of general revenue available for training, to start a business, to move to another region, to share in community controlled job creation projects, and have fishermen's benefits continue.
They also propose that the Unemployment Insurance Commission be an autonomous organization accountable to Parliament through the Minister and to the proprietors of that program, that is the workers and employers who pay for it. Furthermore, in addition to reforming unemployment insurance we need much more vigorous job creation programs; not cut-backs but expansion. Disadvantaged groups such as women returning to the workforce, native people on or off the reserve and youth entering the work-force must be better funded than the token programs being offered now.

May 19, 1987
Supply
Third, one of the serious causes of our present high rate of unemployment is the cut-backs and freezes in public employment. For doctrinaire capitalist reasons the Government and most provincial Governments are withholding work opportunities in the provision of social housing, education, especially post-secondary education, in preventive and environmental health, in child care which the Government has put off and put off and put off and does not want to discuss seriously, and in culture and recreation which has been grossly underfunded compared to most other countries. This policy must be reversed and employment in these services must be increased. These services are in fact essential to a modern industrial and commercial country. Without them our society cannot survive let alone produce efficiently.
If you want to see what happens to a country that follows the road of cut-back and freeze you can find a gruesome example in Chile. Pinochet, using the Chicago Boys' philosophy, has brought about an absolute reduction in the number of children in elementary school although the population is one-sixth larger. There is nearly 50 per cent malnutrition among children under six. There has been a doubling of the rate of some infectious diseases, and massive poverty in what was once a prosperous democracy. The only industry thriving there is the military, people who are needed to repress the poor, the workers and the students.
That brings me to the question of Canada's national defence establishment and arms industry. The Government, by trying to follow President Reagan, is in danger of locking Canada into a defence and defence industry policy that would give us the least security and the least sovereignty at the greatest expense. Worship of high-tech schemes like immense radar systems, nuclear submarines, and star wars, lock us into the American war program, and the continued production in Canada of nuclear fuel with the excuse of nuclear power is wasting billions of tax dollars of which the Oerlikon scandal is only a very small part. As defence these programs are questionable and dangerous since they heat up the arms race and make World World III, an unwinnable war, more likely than ever before. As job creation projects they are a sick joke because dollar for dollar they give us less jobs than any other industry, public or private. By spreading the dictatorial role of the military and the rule of secrecy over more and more of the economy, they are undermining our democracy. By starving public projects of funding, they are impoverishing our people and even our industries. Subsidized arms production for export only compounds the problem.
We need those tax dollars for much better programs. There are many urgently needed public projects that private enterprise, the darling of the Government, will not or cannot do. It is well known that our cities are falling into disrepair. Roads, bridges, sewers, waterworks and other basic necessities are wearing out. The federal Government, which helped to build them in the first place through direct grants and generous tax breaks for real estate development, now looks the other way
and tells the municipalities and provinces that they are on their own.
How extremely shortsighted. If this Government would add $1 billion per year to the $2 billion proposed by the cities and the provinces, nearly all of it would come back to the federal Government in unemployment insurance benefit savings and in new tax dollars. Our cities would be more efficient and this would generate a more efficient economy. Above all, 60,000 more self-respecting Canadians would be working at useful jobs for decent wages. Yet the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) is so obsessed with his paper deficit that he would rather see those 60,000 Canadians unemployed.
In addition, Canada's transportation industries need to be renovated. The railways are worn out. The bus system needs to be expanded. Our air system which is in better shape needs the continuing security of a proper system of regulation, with public ownership, especially of airports. However, besides supplying the essential services and the infrastructure that private enterprise cannot supply satisfactorily, we need to democratize the production of primary and secondary products.
In The Financial Post of June, there appeared an article by Peter Cook entitled: "If We're So Smart, Where are the Jobs?" His subtitle note is as follows:
Countries as diverse as Japan and Sweden have kept unemployment below 4
per cent. Ours is three times higher. What do they know that we don't?
He points out that in spite of 4 per cent growth for four and maybe five years, Canada still has an official national unemployment rate of 9.5 per cent, a combination he calls unprecedented. On the other hand, in Japan where many companies have a commitment to life-time employment, he finds that a laid-off assembly line worker can be switched into the marketing department, sent to a dealership to help reduce inventory or be given a repair job in the plant. Job security like that reduces unnecessary labour market conflict and assists efficient production.
In his other example, Sweden, Cook notes that after 49 years of Social Democratic rule during the last 55 years and a public sector that by 1982 absorbed 67 per cent of Gross Domestic Product, "Growth has averaged 3 per cent to 4 per cent, inflation is down at 3 per cent, the balance of payments is solidly in surplus and unemployment is a mere 2.7 per cent". He finds that while the Swedish Social Democrat Government has refused to prop up lame-duck industries, it has intervened chiefly in the labour market, "to facilitate the transfer of workers from old to new industries and, through high taxes, ensure as much labour mobility as possible". He also says that differences in wage levels in Sweden are small and that if they get large, they get taxed away. As a result of this egalitarianism, Cook says the workers can move to new jobs without facing, as they would in Canada, large differences in living costs and they are helped with retraining and moving costs.
Peter Cook provides a warning which I hope this Government will take to heart. He said:
May 19, 1987

When Sweden got into trouble, it was because, under a conservative coalition,
it departed from its socialist model. In the late 1970s, the government decided
to prop up ailing shipyards and steel works and to spend massively on
subsidized industry-
As we all know, the Social Democrats are back in the driver's seat in Sweden and Cook reports contentedly that they have been retrenching and getting back to basics since. He says that the most flexible labour market among 18 industrial countries is that of Sweden.
In the time I have left, I hope to offer two different parts of Canada as examples of attempting to apply the principles of fair treatment of workers and wages, training, job security and local democratic control.
In Newfoundland, the unemployment rate is as high as 20.4 per cent, the highest, I believe, of any Canadian province. Newfoundland has been richly endowed with fisheries, game, forests, minerals and hydro potential. Unfortunately for the people of Newfoundland, others took control.
In centuries past, the cod fishery in Newfoundland generated its own surplus capital, but as much as two-thirds of that capital was taken away to England. It was not available to build up the economic, social and educational foundations needed by the Newfoundland people.
Likewise, splendid forests were cut down to build large wooden ships, most of which became the property of merchants in England. In second-growth forests, the pulp and paper industry drained off to Britain and the United States the capital resources created by Newfoundland labour, capital resources that ought to have been used to build up a modern Newfoundland.
Mines like the huge iron deposit at Belle Isle and the hydro such as that at Churchill Falls also enriched a few people, mainly in Montreal, New York and perhaps Toronto. This was done at the cost of starving Newfoundland's economic development. No wonder Newfoundland serves employers in central Canada and elsewhere by providing a handy reservoir of the reserve army of labour, the unemployed.
The present Government of Newfoundland is considering a path of job creation that does not rely chiefly on grandiose multimillion-dollar projects of ripping out natural resources and shipping them away as fast as possible along with the future means of living of Newfoundland's children. The Government proposes to concentrate on smaller local projects, viable agriculture for local markets with the help of modern technology and provision of repair, construction and even light industry such as would be proportionate to local financial means and local markets.
The other area to which I would like to refer is Spadina. A local advisory council on employment has been established in Spadina. Many observers find that Canada is becoming deindustrialized and that the bank towers and the fast-food outlets in Spadina cannot take up all the slack in unemployment. Therefore, we in Spadina have focused on the garment
Supply
or fashion industry, on the very substantial hospitality industry and on the busy arts and drama industry.
I give credit to the present Government for having half of a good idea. It has promoted the formation of local advisory councils on unemployment. It was a good hunch to urge local workers' organizations, business organizations, social, cultural and ethnic groups and even politicians to meet together regularly in order to identify local employment needs and to devise workable solutions. Unfortunately, the Government failed to provide either the staff to give continuity to the work of volunteers in searching out necessary labour market information, or the adequate attention of the Minister himself. Vital information about cuts in federal training course allocations was withheld from the local advisory council for nine months. The Minister failed to answer serious questions.
Last May, on the motion of the local advisory council, I wrote the Minister asking that the designation of skills shortages be restored to the title "power sewing operator". Sewing machine operators are vital to the garment industry and that skill is taught at George Brown College which is located in Spadina. Ninety per cent of the graduates of that course had been employed in that trade immediately after graduation, yet the number of places in the course was cut although employers were being held back in production for lack of as many as 200 trained sewing machine operators.
The Minister wrote back in July saying that the course was reduced for lack of applicants. However, his letter pointedly ignored our specific question about the skills designation category. The problem was that potential applicants who did not fit into other programs would have fit under the skills shortage designation but were prevented from doing that. Having prevented them from entering the course, the Government could say it was cutting back on the number of seats in the course for lack of applicants.
The picture of the Minister's ignorance and neglect is much worse than that. In April of this year, after receiving the long-delayed information about the skills shortage designation list, I wrote to the Minister pointing out that he had totally wiped out seven of the eight courses needed for training workers in the fashion industry. He had also wiped out six of the eight courses needed in the hospitality industry, including cooks, in an area with an extremely high concentration of hotels and good restaurants.
Finally, he had wiped out 22 of the 23 courses in the arts, drama and culture industries leaving only "opera singer". In other words, a garment worker or hospitality worker who wants to find a job had better become an opera singer. I am awaiting the Minister's reply without much hope of hearing informed common sense.
I have offered a few thoughts on a practical approach to job creation. The main principle is that we must trust the people of whom the majority are workers. Let them take part in the

May 19, 1987
Supply
planning and decision-making. Assure them of a fair reward and job security and our economic ills can be overcome. We can have a healthy economy and a just society in which people can walk the streets without fearing either unemployment or increased crime as a result of poverty. It can be done. It has been done in other countries. We have done it in Canada before. I hope the Minister will change his policy and begin to follow a well-proven path.

There are questions about the methods used in the seal hunt, but that is not the issue. The issue is the existence of the seal hunt as the only source of revenue for many people in that region. Our position is that it should be replaced with a better way of earning a living, but, until it is, it should continue under the best conditions possible for human and beast.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-UI REFORM-FULL EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Resuming debate. The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard).

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-UI REFORM-FULL EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to take part in the debate today, considering the fact that the decision we announced last week is basically attuned to the economic and social realities in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, the unemployment insurance system, and I think it would do no harm to recall this fact, is essentially based on a partnership that was established in an attempt to meet the needs of Canadians generally and, as far as possible, the specific needs of each individual Canadian. Workers, employers and the Government all contribute towards financing the unemployment insurance fund.
Over ten million Canadians are covered by unemployment insurance and have a vested interest in the administration and the future of the system. Basically, they are insured against job loss as a result of layoffs, termination of employment, sickness or maternity leave. Every day, the system helps hundreds of thousands of Canadians to maintain a minimum income.
To do so, Mr. Speaker, the plan's present structure must reflect the realities of this country's economy. In any discussion on unemployment insurance, we must never forget the diversity that is the strength of this country, but which also means that needs vary from region to region. The unemployment insurance system must and, in fact, does take these regional differences into account.
Mr. Speaker, the unemployed are not confined to one and the same region. The Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap) was referring to the fact that even Toronto had its unemployment problem. However, the problems of the unemployed in Fredericton are not the same as those of the unemployed in Toronto or Vancouver. I think that if we ignore these differences, we are not being realistic. The differences exist, and I think the system must take these into account.

May 19, 1987
Supply
Mr. Speaker, a system based on the concept that we are dealing with a uniform problem could well turn out to be a system that is basically rigid and totally lacking in flexibility. For instance-and I believe I share the concern that has arisen in the past few months in Canada with respect to annualization-if we were to lose $2 billion in unemployment insurance benefits, I think we all realize this would have a disproportionate and damaging impact on regions with a fragile economy.
Workers would not be alone in suffering the impact of such a measure, since the entire economy of the regions in question would be affected, and I think this is a fact the Government is certainly not denying, and a fact that was considered in assessing the system.
Mr. Speaker, as we said last Friday, our consultations have shown that there are in this country two very much polarized positions on unemployment insurance. 1 think we know them quite well. There are those, like the Hon. Member for the Liberal Party whose position, and his was certainly not clear, as usual, is that the program ought to be expanded, while many Canadians-and I don't think we can ignore this fact, which I found came to the fore this morning in a number of interviews-consider that the system should be made more restrictive. I think the findings of the Forget Commission, the Parliamentary Committee, the Newfoundland House Report and the Macdonald Commission, I think that all these groups finally advocated one position or another, but we must admit that most of the major commissions-Forget, Hawkes, the Macdonald Commission-did favour restrictive measures, among others the Forget Commission recommendation which would have reduced unemployment benefits by up to S3 billion, as we know. And so we came to the conclusion that, since each of the various positions is so radical and leaves no room for compromise, the best approach is to maintain the existing system because it best meets the needs of Canadians under present circumstances.
Some people claim that the Forget Commission was a waste of money, yet it is a lot better to have a study confirming that the system we have, although it has its weak points, is best suited to the situation than to change things just for the sake of changing, or to say that because we paid $6 million for a study we have to spend $1 billion if only because a commission cannot be asked to make a study without recommending changes. Why? Why can a study not reveal that the system we have is the best one available?
We looked at the recommendations to expand the program. We looked at the benefits and the costs. To spend $1 billion or more to enrich the program would not have been in the best interests of the partnership and could have a negative effect on our economic recovery. To increase the benefits, to make benefits easier to get, to pay benefits for a longer period of time, would undeniably change UI. However, a bigger program is not necessarily a better program. An increase in the
scope and coverage of the program would result in a corresponding increase in the cost of the program.
Let us take an example. To lower the entrance requirements for all workers to 10 weeks and to provide an automatic 50 weeks of benefits would cost more than $500 million. This would not improve the over-all program. It would offer more benefits to some workers but would increase premiums for all workers and for all employers. It would increase disincentives to work and to make the program rigid to the detriment of the entire labour market.
I do not believe that workers would rather collect UI than have meaningful employment. The vast majority of Canadians want work first. Yes, there are those people for whom this is not true. There are those who abuse the system and in so doing cheat their fellow workers. However, the solution to this problem is not to wield an axe and cut benefits for all workers across the country. The approach must be specific and precise. As we announced on Friday, we intend to modestly increase our efforts to weed out the abusers by, for instance, seeing that claimants are interviewed more often by more officers to ensure that they are looking for work and are accepting suitable job opportunities.
We have looked at suggestions to cut the program by $2 billion or $3 billion or more, but this would seriously undermine the ability of UI to properly protect Canadian workers. We will not impose such hardship.
The study we have made of unemployment insurance shows that while UI is not perfect, it is a fundamentally sound program. Unemployment insurance not only provides a substantial response but a swift response to changing labour market conditions. It responds directly to individual needs and in so doing assists local economies and the national economy. Both dramatic cuts and dramatic increases carry with them undesirable consequences. Neither promises better than the current broad program. The uemployment insurance program is a balanced national program meeting the needs of individuals and communities across the country.

The Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand) who moved today's motion is usually a well-informed man. Although on this side of the House at the time, he was a Member when Canada's unemployment rates peaked, when interest rates were soaring and the economy was stagnant, but of course this was due to the crisis, it was somebody else's fault. Generally speaking the Liberal Party never did accept responsibility for the economic situation of 1983-84, yet it did create it. Mr. Speaker, suffice to say that Canadians passed judgment on the economic management of the previous administration.
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East knows full well that unemployment insurance did Canadians a good service before the recession. He also knows that unemployment insurance plays a vital role on the labour market. However it is only one aspect of the
May 19, 1987

efforts made by the Government to help Canadians face the new economic conditions.
Last Friday I stated that the trade, tax and economic policies as well as the regional and human resources development policies were basically aimed at helping Canadians find stable employment. My colleague knows that all these measures have contributed to strengthen the economy, restore confidence and create jobs. A lot of things may appear doubtful, but 800,000 real jobs, 85 per cent of stable jobs are not dreams but facts. Not only have we made progress, but I think we are also building a solid foundation for years of growth, prosperity and employment for new Canadians, such as the co-operation offered in that respect by the Hon. Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps). I think we will have jobs for these future Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, the work done by my Department attests to the commitments we made and fits in nicely with initiatives taken in other sectors. Employment planning, to be specific, is based on the strength of the economic growth and makes it even more dynamic. Let us not forget that we are not talking about abstractions but about the needs of individuals, about concrete realities. In all regions of the country, and I suggest this is the big plus about employment planning, it is geared to the person, to the requirements and basic needs of individuals. Practically all programs of previous administrations had been based on labour market theories and presented in attractive manuals which were the latest fad several decades earlier. According to the theory applied by the previous Government, labour market problems fell into certain categories, depending on the factors that caused them. They were either cyclical, seasonal or structural. Cyclical factors were connected with the economic cycle, seasonal factors with the seasonal drop in employment and structural factors essentially reflected the imbalance between the skills in demand on the market, and the skills workers had to offer.
Mr. Speaker, the old programs focused on what were seen as the causes of employment problems, but unfortunately, the labour market does not work like that. It does not operate according to specific rules. In Canada, unemployment has remained high for some time. Although the general situation has improved over the last two years, long term unemployment remains a problem. In this kind of context, the creation of short term jobs is pretty useless as far as most of the country is concerned.
Today, it is impossible to pinpoint one specific cause for a worker's being unemployed. It is more important to give workers a chance to acquire the skills and experience actually in demand on the labour market. The jobs strategy is therefore aimed above all at those who are most in need of employment assistance, whatever the economic cause of the problem. The strategy provides for various combinations of courses, training on the job and practical experience, so as to provide the formula that is best suited to a particular region, community or individual.
Supply
Mr. Speaker, increasingly, people are realizing that the best way to help those who need employment assistance consists in offering them a combination of institutional training and practical experience, while avoiding any rigid distinction between these two types of training. We must remove the barriers between the world of labour and that of education. We want to bring on-the-job training and formal school education closer together, and bridge the gap which still exists between a great many of our labour market training institutions. Employment planning can provide the essential flexibility which Canada needs to adapt to the rapidly changing labour market.
Major changes are taking place in the work place because of technological and market transformations. In an ever-changing situation, programs must adapt and the decision-making process must be extended at the regional or local level, which is the reason behind the existence of local employment committees where such changes are immediately identified.
I am pleased to report that it is a challenge to which Canadians are responding in increasing numbers. Although it is only 18 months since this fundamental change was introduced, more than 400,000 Canadians have benefited from the skills and experience gained through the six options of Jobs Strategy.
Another fundamental change has been the Government's commitment to continually monitor, assess and re-evaluate the program. We cannot and will not assume that what worked yesterday is also the solution for tomorrow. We have established mechanisms to determine the performance of each program. Our aim is clear-we want to eliminate what does not work, to improve what does work and to anticipate continually future needs.
The preliminary results of our first surveys of our programs are really most encouraging. Results show that the entry and re-entry options report success rates of 73 per cent for young people who completed entry and 67 per cent for women completing re-entry. These are good figures. They show that we already have improvement over the 64 per cent success rate of old-style institutional training in the same period.
Results are equally positive with respect to employment equity. Participation of women, natives, the disabled and visible minorities are all higher than under the programs that preceded the Canadian Jobs Strategy. Most targets for women have already been met in the first year of operation.
We have also conducted follow-up studies which reveal an overwhelmingly positive response among participants. Fully 89 per cent said that their participation in the Jobs Strategy provided them with new or better employment or helped them to retain their present jobs.
The results are encouraging. They point to the essential value of the changes we have made. They will not serve as

May 19, 1987
Supply
laurels upon which we rest. Rather, they are spurs to our continuing efforts to assist individuals, communities and regions across the country.
The labour market is not static. Fully 2 million Canadians leave and enter the labour market each year. Such changes and adjustments occur every day. Every sector of Canada plays a part in this dynamic process.

Mr. Speaker, the Government is simply trying to facilitate and integrate the efforts of teaching institutions within the private sector to meet the needs of both the business world and labour organizations, as well as voluntary groups and individuals.
Thanks to the updating of resources, solutions are coming to light in every region, every community, every corporation, and from each and every individual.
In short, Mr. Speaker, our unemployment insurance scheme is providing good results. We have never claimed it to be perfect, and past studies have not striven for perfection either. However, in the consideration of various commissions, various studies that were made, it has been useful in my view to receive all those recommendations which enabled us to realize that the proposed change . . . Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East suggested earlier we should take a proposal here, another proposal there. They were very careful not to say they supported the Forget Report. Of course, they prefer to quote selectively from the Forget Report.
Mr. Speaker, when there is a report with an overall impact that one cannot implement, one cannot choose one bit from a report, another bit from another report, and try to make some sort of melting pot that does not meet today's reality. We have decided the current system in the circumstances was the best one because of that impossibility. And if there is one conclusion to be derived from the Canadian Jobs Strategy, it is that while it is important to provide solid protection to the unemployed, temporary protection under which they can look for a job, the Government first and foremost, and in this we are successful, the Government should first ensure it provides jobs. Such is the goal of the Jobs Strategy. The results are there. Results are now increasingly encouraging, and all we ask is an opportunity to carry on while again protecting workers who unfortunately lose their jobs.

Mir. Allmand: Mr. Speaker, in his remarks the Minister said that we should not implement a report simply because it cost $7 million. I agree with him on that point. Reports are not implemented simply because they cost a large amount of money. However, I do not think we should reject an entire report simply because there are opposing views on different recommendations.
I wish to ask the Minister this. Why would he not introduce those measures with respect to which there is common ground, such as a wider scope for training while on unemployment
insurance, changes in maternity benefits to make them parental benefits in certain cases and some changes with respect to over-payments?
The Minister said that I have never declared myself for or against the Forget Report. There are 53 recommendations in the report. In all my years here I have never seen a report in which all recommendations were either accepted or rejected. Governments pick and choose those recommendations which they believe to be practical and possible and they reject others. Within a few weeks after the Forget Report came out the Minister himself made a decision with respect to cuts relating to pre-retired pensioners. We may have disagreed or agreed with his decision, but we did not condemn him for not dealing with the entire report at one time. So I ask him why he will not accept those recommendations on which there is common ground.
I wish to return to the recommendation with respect to a wider scope for training. It is a recommendation which would not even cost more money to implement. All that is required to implement it is a change in the law. In order to permit those who were on unemployment insurance to take a wider range of training programs we amended the law a few years ago. But we now find that it is not enough. Both the standing committee and Mr. Forget recommended that while one is on unemployment insurance there should be a wider scope for training. I will not get into the details in my question, but why can the Minister not move in those areas by bringing a Bill forward? I mentioned about eight areas in which there are common ground and where there is agreement, not on the details but in principle. I believe that we could do a great deal to improve unemployment insurance by acting on these recommendations.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-UI REFORM-FULL EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member has posed an interesting question. We believe that any kind of reform that deals with the scope, the costs of the program, does not have to be considered for the moment. The standing committee mentioned a cost of $1 billion. Of course, the Hon. Member has other figures. But we could talk about a cost of at least $500 million. The Member has referred to training services being provided under the unemployment insurance system. While that could be a logical move, we believe it could lead to too great a widening of the program itself.
For most Canadians the UI system has to be just that, an insurance plan. However, increasingly for some it has become a part of the social welfare system. That is not a trend that I necessarily condemn. That aspect of the unemployment insurance system is an important one in those regions of the country where the economy is so fragile. But, to broaden the scope of the UI system in order to achieve better results in those areas could lead to other problems.

subsubtopic: INTERNMENT OF JAPANESE CANADIANS DURING WORLD WAR II-PROPOSAL TO RESOLVE ISSUE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the inability of the Government to reach a fair and appropriate agreement on the issue of Japanese Canadian redress was most regrettable. The Government failed, during this heightened window of opportunity, to right a long-standing wrong.
Its failure, however, was inevitable and predictable, for the Conservative administration steadfastly refused to attach to this issue the political priority it deserved, and refused to establish a comprehensive process for dialogue.
Moreover, this stubborn and short-sighted attitude makes a mockery of the personal commitment of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) to the issue. He promised urgency. He promised compensation. He promised negotiations. Yet, through three different Conservative Ministers of Multicultur-alism, the National Association of Japanese Canadians was resigned to individual meetings here and there, sessions which were not conducive to a spirit of compromise, to a spirit of give and take, or to a spirit of understanding.
Instead the Government entrenched an adversarial approach, pitting the Government against the Japanese Canadian community, while opposition Parties and parliamentarians were totally ignored and kept in the dark.
I call upon the Minister and the Government to give the process a chance. A sensitive process is needed to reach a resolution of what is a very sensitive and pressing national issue.

subtopic: TWO-PRICE WHEAT SYSTEM-INCREASE IN ONTARIO PRODUCTION FOR DOMESTIC CONSUMPTION
TWO-PRICE WHEAT SYSTEM-INCREASE IN ONTARIO PRODUCTION FOR DOMESTIC CONSUMPTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canada's two-price wheat policy pays Canadian farmers $7 per bushel for the 10 per cent of Canadian wheat production which goes into domestic human consumption. The traditional split in the domestic wheat benefit has been
approximately 87 per cent to the Canadian Wheat Board area and 13 per cent to Ontario and the rest of Canada.
Ontario production of good quality red wheat can be sold straight to the miller at the domestic price, thus giving Ontario producers the potential to displace production from western Canada. This spring Ontario producers have increased their red spring wheat acreage by 400 per cent, a pattern which, if magnified, could seriously upset the historical regional balance in the two-price wheat benefit.
I urge the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer) to note the report of the 1986 special committee on the pricing of domestic wheat, which recommended that he explore mechanisms to ensure that the two-price wheat policy continues to reflect the historic regional market share of all wheat types used domestically for human consumption.
This benefit should be available to producers regardless of where they live or who sells their wheat.

subtopic: CALL FOR RESIGNATIONS TO FACILITATE ESTABLISHMENT OF ELECTED SENATE
CALL FOR RESIGNATIONS TO FACILITATE ESTABLISHMENT OF ELECTED SENATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) has come up with what he has called an ingenious way of moving toward an elected Senate, a proposal which has the support of Alberta, Saskatchewan, and Manitoba Liberal Parties.
The Hon. Member proposes that prairie Premiers hold elections to determine their nominees for any future vacancies in the Senate. This return to democratic principles by the Liberal Parties of western Canada is overdue.
Might I make a suggestion of how the Liberals could show that they are serious about it, not simply trying to exploit the movement toward an elected Senate, a movement which has its origins, in large part, in the failure of Liberal Senators from the West, and western Liberals in general, to understand and meet the needs of western Canada during their many years in government?
My suggestion would be equally ingenious. It would be that the 12 Liberals in the Senate from western Canada who are now clogging up that place, resign en masse, this dirty dozen, and make a significant advance toward an elected Senate immediately possible. Instead, what the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry suggested would simply be a vacancy by vacancy advance well into the 21st Century.
If the Liberal Members in the other place would do that, perhaps we could take the Liberals seriously.

May 19, 1987
