subtopic: DEMAND THAT NATIONAL ANTHEM BE SUNG IN BOTH OFFICIAL LANGUAGES AT EDMONTON OILERS' HOCKEY GAMES
DEMAND THAT NATIONAL ANTHEM BE SUNG IN BOTH OFFICIAL LANGUAGES AT EDMONTON OILERS' HOCKEY GAMES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Sunday, that is on May 17, the final series of the Stanley Cup between the Edmonton Oilers and the Philadephia Flyers began. The Oilers organization which I am pleased to congratulate had chosen a francophone, Mr. Loriaux, to sing the Canadian and American anthems.
In view of the fact that hockey is recognized as our sport and the overwhelming majority of spectators of that game were French-speaking and English-speaking Canadians, it was entirely proper to expect that O Canada would be sung in both French and English. However, such was not the case and it was only sung in English.
I do not know why but I feel that this is unacceptable and I ask the Oilers organization in Edmonton to reconsider the matter and ensure that French is also used at the opening of Stanley Cup games.

subtopic: HELICOPTER ACCIDENT IN OUTAOUAIS-CONDOLENCES TO FAMILIES

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: HELICOPTER ACCIDENT IN OUTAOUAIS-CONDOLENCES TO FAMILIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a tragic accident occurred over the weekend when the helicopter chartered by Hull's station CHOT snagged a power cable as a crew was shooting sequences for a hunting and fishing program at Grand Lake, killing all five aboard.
On behalf of the Liberal Party and all my colleagues in the House I should like to offer my most sincere condolences to the families of Messrs. Jacques Beriault, Claude Girard, Clement Diotte and Guy Frechette of CHOT station, and to the family of pilot Jean-Paul Parent. They made up an outstanding crew working to keep the National Capital Region public better informed and thus making it possible for station CHOT to maintain its rating of excellence and popularity among French regional stations.
Again I offer my most sincere condolences to the families and to their station CHOT TV colleagues.

subtopic: PROPOSED MOTION INCORPORATING PROTECTION FOR UNBORN CHILDREN
PROPOSED MOTION INCORPORATING PROTECTION FOR UNBORN CHILDREN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Motion M-37, sponsored by the Hon. Member for Grey-Simcoe (Mr. Mitges), asks that the Charter of Rights and Freedoms be amended so as to protect the unborn human foetus. I and millions of Canadians support this protection for the unborn child.
I believe life begins upon conception and I base this conviction on Scripture which is the word inspired by our omnipotent God. For example, from the Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 1, verse 5: "Before I formed you in the womb I knew you; and before you were were born I consecrated you."
Some 60,000 unborn babies are murdered every year in Canada. Cradled in the mother's womb should be the safest place in the world for a child, but not in Canada; certainly not for the 60,000 who were aborted during the last 12 months.
Not one Member of this House would be here today had our mothers chosen abortion. I urge every Member to give unborn babies in Canada a chance to live by passing Motion M-37.

subtopic: IMPORTANCE OF WORK OF LIGHTHOUSE KEEPERS
IMPORTANCE OF WORK OF LIGHTHOUSE KEEPERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in 1984 a federal inquiry headed by Paul Leblond said that lightkeepers are the only source of information on local weather conditions available to mariners. Their contributions are invaluable. Three years later the Government has again enlisted Dr. Leblond to investigate the impact of the Tory plan to destaff a number of West Coast light stations.
While search and rescue activities are not part of their job description, lighthouse keepers have recorded numerous rescue incidents. How many of these incidents were serious enough to be called life threatening? How many lives is the Government willing to risk?
The assault on Canada's light stations started under the former Liberal Government. Between 1978 and 1985 the number of person-years allocated to light stations declined by approximately 200. In the name of restraint the present Government has taken this scheme further and now plans to replace workers with machines.
Last week one of the witnesses told the Leblond inquiry that automation is a hazard to navigation. We need real modernization of lighthouses and not automation which is unreliable at best.
May 19, 1987

[ Translation]

Mr. Speaker, today is the centenary of engineering in Canada. For 100 years Canada has been relying on the brains of its residents to ensure its progress.
What would we be today without our Canadian engineers? Without them, where would we rank in research, science and technology?
Canadian engineers have become the driving force behind our development and earned a worldwide reputation. We often see a Canadian heading a major project in other countries of the world. Our engineers are the best and we are proud of them.
I want to thank Canada Post Corporation management for issuing today a commemorative stamp marking the one-hundredth year of engineering in Canada, and 1 urge all Canadian Members of Parliament who are engineers to join me on this historic event.

subtopic: ALLEGED INTENTION OF GOVERNMENT TO WITHDRAW FROM FIELD
ALLEGED INTENTION OF GOVERNMENT TO WITHDRAW FROM FIELD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Le Devoir newspaper informed us this morning that the Government intends to withdraw from regional development. This announcement comes after a series of measures taken by this Government which show its lack of interest in fighting regional disparities. I suggest that one of the most important things for this Parliament and Canada as a whole is to make sure that citizens are given equal opportunities, wherever they may live in this country. We have come to realize that with its free enterprise philosophy, the Government is completely abdicating its responsibility of ensuring that people of far-away and disadvantaged areas have equal access to employment and dignity.
Mr. Speaker, I feel it will be a very sad day when the Government of Canada abdicates all its responsibilities and says to the less affluent regions: Take care of your own problems. Mr. Speaker, I think that after having promised the moon to the Canadian people and assuring all regions of equal access, the Conservative Government has again broken one of its promises, thereby jeopardizing the very survival of economic equality in Canada.

subtopic: FOREIGN INVESTMENT-NEED FOR CANADIAN CONTENT REQUIREMENT
FOREIGN INVESTMENT-NEED FOR CANADIAN CONTENT REQUIREMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, North American car manufacturers are tied into a trade pact providing for a 60 per cent Canadian value added. Offshore car plants are expected to assemble about 430,000 new cars per year in Canada by the year 1990 and are not subject to the same limitations or to any requirement to source supply in Canada. The only possible result can be a loss of Canadian jobs in the Canadian auto parts supply sector and even more in the assembly plants when North American manufacturers turn to foreign-built cars which are sold in Canada under recognized trade names.
I call on the Government now to review its foreign investment policy to ensure the strengthening of the Canadian automobile industry and to ensure that foreign investment must be an investment in Canadian jobs.

subtopic: COST OF CANADIAN WOMEN BECOMING SURROGATE PARENTS
COST OF CANADIAN WOMEN BECOMING SURROGATE PARENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canada is experiencing a Baby M dilemma of its own with an added twist. Americans are now using Canadian women as surrogate mothers with medicare benefits thrown in for good measure.
Growing numbers of American couples find that by using Canadian women as surrogate mothers, the cost of surrogate parenting is lowered. The dollar amount has been estimated at around $5,000 per birth which is paid by the Canadian taxpayer.
Are we to allow people from foreign lands to exploit our medicare system for personal benefit and gain? Furthermore, this raises the whole question of the contracting of parental responsibility.
It is clear that the American Baby M case does not affect contract law in Canada but we must now ask the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) to introduce into Parliament the Government's clear position on the issue of surrogate parenting.
As science moves quickly, so do expanded roles for surrogate parents. This raises a number of questions, paramount of which is the interest of the child. Are the interests of children being served? I daresay they may not be and I think the Minister of Justice should show some leadership in this area.

May 19, 1987

subtopic: AID GIVEN TO INCO AND GOLDEN KNIGHT RESOURCES
AID GIVEN TO INCO AND GOLDEN KNIGHT RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Abitibi area will experience a new mineral resources development through the opening of a new gold field. I am referring to the first stage in the development of the Golden Pond East gold deposit, situated in the Casa Berardi township in the federal riding of Abitibi, some 100 kilometers north of La Sarre, on the Villebois-Selbaie-Joutel highway.
Assistance amounting to $14.5 million has been granted to Inco Ltd. and its partner, the Golden Knight Resources Ltd, to be shared equally by the Governments of Canada and Quebec under the infrastructure program provided for by the Canada-Quebec Subsidiary Agreement on Mineral Developments. It will be used to build an access route and a high-voltage power line in this faraway region. This project will necessitate over $74 million in investments and create some 180 jobs when production starts in 1988.
As elected representative of that region, I am proud, together with the Hon. Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Masse) and the Hon. Minister of State (Forestry and Mines) (Mr. Merrithew), to share in this major development in a remote mining territory.

Mr. Speaker, last week we had another example of the double standards used by the United States in the matter of foreign investment when their country is involved rather than Canada. Recently, Dominion Textiles in Montreal announced it was ready to make a bid for the Burlington Industries in Greenberg, North Carolina. But that company was not interested in using State politicians from North Carolina and Members of the American Senate to fight against the Canadian take over. It is amusing, Mr. Speaker, that while the Americans are looking for free investment access in Canada, it appears the North Carolina Assembly put in place legislation to block the purchase of an American Corporation by a Canadian company. We may sympathize with American politicians, Mr. Speaker, since foreign ownership in the United States, including the textile industry, could lead to a loss of jobs and technology. But this is something we Canadians know. For that reason we want to protect our interests, our industries and we are asking the Americans not to apply double standards.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to draw the attention of the House to the special needs of the 38,000 visually impaired people living in Canada today. While most of us jot down a phone message on a piece of paper, a blind person must often purchase and use a recording device. Special equipment is also needed for reading and writing.
Many blind people depend upon public transit, but in smaller centres that can be a problem when buses run infrequently and never on Sundays. Consequently, blind people must often take taxis and that is expensive. In short, Mr. Speaker, it costs money to be blind.
Meeting the special needs of the blind can also be costly in the workplace and many employers are unwilling or unable to buy the equipment necessary to hire a blind person. This results in lost work opportunities for people who are capable of doing a job but are denied the right to work because they are visually impaired.
The federal Government has already substantially improved the situation of handicapped Canadians but more needs to be done to remove the economic obstacles which blind people now have to deal with at home and in the workplace.

speakeroldname: Hon. David Crombie (Secretary of State of Canada):

subsubtopic: INTERNMENT OF JAPANESE CANADIANS DURING WORLD WAR II-PROPOSAL TO RESOLVE ISSUE

Mr. Speaker, during the last seven months I suppose I engaged in the order of 20 to 30 meetings on this issue. That is pretty sensitive dialogue. All Members of this House should know the net result was that for the first time a Government of Canada said it would acknowledge the injustice of the treatment of the Japanese Canadian community in the 1940s. We stand ready to do that today.
Second, in my letter of March 27 I indicated we would repeal the War Measures Act and make sure those injustices would not occur again under its replacement.
Where we do not yet have common ground is on the question of money-not on the moral principle but on the question of money. We offered a $12 million fund which would produce $1 million to $1.5 million each year for that community. The executive of the National Association of Japanese Canadians is still demanding over $400 million. We have no common ground on the question of money.

In that way, together with the Japanese Canadian community, all three Parties can harness their efforts to try to reach a settlement of this issue which would do honour to Parliament and all Canadians. Every Member of Parliament would like to resolve this issue during the life of this Parliament.

speakeroldname: Hon. David Crombie (Secretary of State of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for Multiculturalism; Secretary of State of Canada

Mr. Speaker, first, if the committee wants to participate all it need do is so indicate. It has not done that. More importantly, when I first took on this task I met with my critic and two other Members in the NDP who asked me to consider certain facets of this issue. If the Hon. Member, and indeed any member of his caucus, want to participate in this process all they have to do is get in touch with me or the National Association of Japanese Canadians. It seems to me that was open to the Member and his caucus all along.

This morning the Minister and members of the Government were laughing in glee over an unemployment rate of around 9.3 per cent. The Liberal Party does not think a full employment policy is a joke. We think it is an objective toward which we should be working.
I would like to spend a few minutes outlining the lack of a full employment policy of the Government in relation to older workers.

And I know for a fact that there are a number of Hon. Members, Conservative Members, who have indicated an interest for the issue of older workers, and I believe that the Hon. Member for Jonquiere (Mr. Blackburn) has indicated a deep interest for older workers. Member for Jonquiere and other Conservative back-benchers did not have the courage to stand up to the Finance Minister (Mr. Wilson), who had committed himself a year ago to introducing in the House a specific policy for older workers.

We hear government Members making pronouncements on all these issues in committee, yet when the telling moment comes in the House to vote on a resolution, such as the one before the House today, or to confront the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), they are afraid to do so and disappear. We do not hear them speaking out.

Several months before February of 1986 the Government unilaterally and with one fell swoop did away with the Labour Adjustment Benefits Program which was the only program targeted for older workers. Mr. Speaker, according to the most recent statistics on unemployment among older workers, as presented in a March 1987 article entitled Les pertes d'emplois, et adaptation au marche du travail dans I'economie canadienne, it is already an established fact that once they lose their job, these workers, older workers that is, are more likely to leave the labour force. First of all, in January 1986, no less than 42 per cent left the labour force. And second . . .
Second, for those who did remain in the labour force, the job search was longer for older workers than any other age group. When they finally found jobs, those jobs tended to pay much less than the previous employment and much less than the national average.
The job search for the 45 per cent who did locate new fulltime employment was the longest. It took them 33 weeks to find a new job, and the average wage loss between the lost and new full-time job was 12 per cent, also the largest of any age group. Furthermore, the one-half of those workers who took pay cuts lost an average of one-third of their wages in the job change. These pay cuts are likely related to the fact that many of these older workers lack levels of education and had already undergone longer than average job searches.

That this House condemn the Government for its failure to initiate meaningful reform in the unemployment insurance system and for its failure to commit itself to a full employment policy that seriously addresses high regional unemployment, youth unemployment, part-time work and labour market adjustment.
The Government literally laughs in the House at our proposal for a full employment policy. I believe the purpose of the motion of the Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace- Lachine East is to make a full employment policy a goal for us all to attempt to achieve.
During his remarks he mentioned how two previous Liberal Governments have been able to keep the level of unemployment below 3 per cent because we set a full employment policy as our first national priority. Yet the Government will not even make a commitment to set 7 per cent, 6 per cent or 5 per cent as a national target for a reduction in unemployment.
We do not expect the Minister or the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) to achieve this goal tomorrow, although the Prime Minister stated during the election campaign that tens of thousands of jobs would be created overnight. It has been over two years since the mandate of the Conservative Government, and the average unemployment rate is higher than it ever was during the tenure of Liberal Governments in the past century.
It is difficult to understand why the Government is not prepared to set the objective of achieving a full employment policy by the end of its mandate. I believe that the Government is so committed to non-intervention and is so free market driven that it believes it has no place in the area of job-creation. This has been illustrated quite clearly in the cutbacks and slashes to the Canadian Jobs Strategy. The Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East outlined the cruel reality of a 30 per cent cut in funds that the Government should make available for job strategy programs.

And today, the Conference Board of Canada provided data which suggest that the situation in all provinces except Ontario and a few parts of Quebec will be worse.

We have heard the dire predictions of the Conference Board with respect to employment. The unemployment situation in certain sections of the Province of Newfoundland is worse than it ever was under the previous Liberal Government. Yet the Government will not make a commitment to a full employment policy.
While I certainly respect the work of government Members on the all-Party committee that came forth with unanimous recommendations dealing with part-time work and the question of unemployment insurance, I believe those Members on the government side who truly believe that there should be some drastic changes in the Government's approach to the unemployed in this country have no choice but to support this motion whole-heartedly. I invite them to do so.
The Minister and the Prime Minister have stated that they want to involve the regions and localities in the decentralization process. Therefore, the Government must begin to give some credence to the recommendations coming from the local advisory councils. The local advisory council in Hamilton is becoming quite frustrated by a Government that consistently ignores the advice of an advisory body that it established. I ask government Members to support this motion which will at least encourage the Government, if it does nothing else in this Parliament, to make a full employment policy its first priority in the goals we attempt to achieve. That will mean that those older workers who so far have been ignored by the Government, and those people who are not working, can have some hope.
If you wish to share our dream, then obviously you must agree with a motion which aims at eliminating unemployment in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I listened to the Hon. Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps), and then I listened to one of the most pompous and arrogant speeches from the Minister of State for Youth (Mr. Charest) that 1 have ever heard in the House.
I should first like to deal with the Liberals. We heard the Hon. Member for Hamilton East and other Liberals talk about the new discovery of a full employment policy. Have we forgotten that their Leader in the previous Government, Pierre Elliott Trudeau, when unemployment was at 6 per cent and rising and when inflation was rising, turned around and said to workers who were demonstrating on the Hill: "If you think 6 per cent is high, you just watch me"? We watched as unemployment sky-rocketed into the teens. Can we believe that is the same Party whose Leader, Pierre Elliott Trudeau, went out to Salmon Arm and, when all the unemployed lined up at the side of the railway tracks, gave them the finger? Did I hear the Hon. Member for Hamilton East bellowing from Hamilton against the policy of high unemployment in order to bring inflation down? Is that their version of employment? They are the same group who allowed interest rates to sky-rocket and caused the recession of 1982. That, in turn, put the unemployment insurance fund into hock for about $3 billion.
Then we listened to the pomposity of the Minister of State for Youth. Was it not his Government who, three short summers ago, in August of 1984, during the election said there are three main issues in this campaign: jobs, jobs, jobs?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-UI REFORM-FULL EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-UI REFORM-FULL EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Here we are in 1987, three years later, and what does the Minister stand up and say? We are changing the base of the economy from resources to technology, and that takes time. Yet today we have over a million people unemployed, and that is only the official figure. The youth in this country are experiencing the highest unemployment rate of any group at more than 20 per cent.
If we look at the regions of this country, leaving Ontario out of it for the moment, unemployment is as high as it was under the previous Liberal Government. Then we look at Ontario. The vast majority of all jobs the Government claims have been created, over 75 per cent, are within a 60 mile radius of Toronto. We in northern Ontario do not experience any of the fall-out from the economic resurgence in Ontario.
It is also very disturbing to note that most of the new jobs are being created in the service sector. That sector is the soft underbelly of the economy in general. For example, in communities that depend on the exploitation of resources, any rumour of a lay-off or actual lay-off immediately results in the shutting down, closing up and laying off of workers in the service sector. Furthermore, the service sector is fragile and pays the lowest wages.
When we hear the Liberals talk about how many resolutions on full employment they passed at their convention, we know what that currency is worth. No sooner had the delegates left for the airport after the convention than their Leader said he is not bound by policies passed by the convention. Over on the other side they do not talk about policies. It is the backroom boys, the Dalton Camps and Lowell Murrays, who sit down and decide what they think Canadians would like to hear. If the Minister thinks they have done such a great job over there, he should know that the public does not have the same myopic vision.
What I have said has a direct bearing on the unemployment insurance program. I want to thank the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand) for putting this motion before the House today. I also want to congratulate the Conservative Members who sat on the Standing Committee on Employment and Immigration. They are the Hon. Member for Willowdale (Mr. Oostrom), the Hon. Member for La Prairie (Mr. Jourdenais), the Hon. Member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Howie), the Hon. Member for Jonquiere (Mr. Blackburn), the Hon. Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes) and the Hon. Member for Hochelaga- Maisonneuve (Mr. Desrosiers). There were six Conservatives, one NDP and one Liberal on that committee.
What was the committee's task? To examine the Forget Commission report and table a response in Parliament in the hope it would guide the Minister in his response on May 15 to that report. There is absolutely no doubt in my mind that when the committee sat down, many Conservative Members were infected by myths concerning unemployment insurance. They were and are myths propagated by the National Citizen's Coalition, a right-wing organization in Canada, the Federation of Independent Business led by John Bulloch, various Chambers of Commerce, the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, and the Construction Association of Canada. These myths were expressed, at first, by Conservative Members on that committee, and I want to discuss them.
Myth number one is that unemployment insurance is generous and abused. In fact, the average benefit in 1987 was $180.69 per week. Extrapolated over a year, that amounts to
May 19, 1987

about $9,000. That is way below the poverty line for a single person and far, far below the poverty line for a married individual with dependent children. 1 hear that the program is abused. All the evidence which came before the committee indicated that abuse made up 3 per cent, and that includes claimants receiving benefits in error. In other words, when the UIC makes a mistake and people collect money in error that is included in the 3 per cent. Yet that 3 per cent compares very well with medicare and legal aid. In addition, some 15 per cent of clients quit their jobs voluntarily. The vast majority have been laid off. That 15 per cent includes those who quit for what is called just cause. If it is not just cause it is good cause.
Then we have the story that there are 10 and 40 wonders out there, that is, people who work for 10 weeks and then quit and collect 40 weeks of benefits. That is a myth. We found out that those people constitute less than 3 per cent of claimants.
The second myth is that people in seasonal industries ought not to be able to collect unemployment insurance. For example, fishermen know they are going to be unemployed for four months in the winter and therefore that is predictable and they ought not to be covered by the program. The same would apply to all seasonal workers. Well, is it or is it not important that the fishing resource of this country be exploited by Canadians? I have not spoken to a fisherman on the East Coast of this country who would not like to fish 12 months of the year. Yet the Government tells them when they are going to fish, where and how much they are going to take. If the Government establishes these limitations on seasonal workers and the Government believes this is a resource that should be exploited for the benefit of Canada, then in fact the Government and society as a whole have a responsibility to ensure that when seasonal fishermen are not fishing, they are not starving and dependent on the community as a whole, and that goes for all seasonal workers.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-UI REFORM-FULL EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Don't forget Mother Nature.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-UI REFORM-FULL EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
The Hon. Minister of National Revenue (Mr. MacKay) has reminded us not to forget Mother Nature. Of course we cannot forget the boss upstairs. He has a say in this. It seems to me that the myth that seasonal workers rip off the unemployment insurance system is simply that, a myth.
Another myth is that we should return to running the Unemployment Insurance Program on true insurance principles. There is the argument that the Unemployment Insurance Program should not be a social insurance program. To do that, we would have to take benefits away from fishermen and seasonal workers and we would have to take away maternity and sick benefits. Any aspect of the program that speaks to the social needs of the working class would be taken out of the Unemployment Insurance Program. If we were to do that, where would we put them? What would we do with a person who is sick but works for a business too small to have a sickness insurance program? I do not care how the facts are
Supply
twisted or turned, the benefits come from one pocket and that is the pocket of the taxpayer.
Those are the myths I have heard consistently. I have heard that UI benefits discourage people from leaving an area with low employment opportunities and moving to an area with high employment opportunities. However, when people move away from an area, the people left in the area that is denuded of workers are told that they do not have a workforce so they cannot attract industry. If the people stay there, they are told that the UIC benefits are keeping them in place and they should go abroad to look for work. We cannot have it both ways.
These are the myths that were prevalent among Tory Members when we were trying to determine our response to the report of the Forget Commission. It was a moving experience for me to see Conservatives, some of whom are to the right of Genghis Khan politically, after listening to the persuasive evidence-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-UI REFORM-FULL EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Easy, now.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-UI REFORM-FULL EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
It certainly was not my eloquence that moved the Conservatives. God give me the grace to move Conservatives. Then every motion I would put to the House would be agreed to unanimously.
I observed Conservatives questioning the witnesses closely day by day, hour by hour, probing with their minds set in the myths they brought to the committee. We heard from witnesses and were provided expert research. Mr. Forget was before the committee twice. We had both the majority and the minority commission reports. We had evidence from both sides of the spectrum. We listened, we questioned and when the dust cleared, we proposed 90 recommendations, three score and 30. Support for 89 of them was unanimous and the majority supported the ninetieth one. Only one Member, the Hon. Member for Jonquiere voted against pension income as UI.
The committee that looked at the Forget report reflected the reality of this Parliament. There were six Conservatives, one NDP and one Liberal. All six Tories voted along with the lone Liberal and the lone New Democrat to support 89 of the recommendations unanimously.
Then the recommendations were tabled in the House. God only knows when the Minister would have found the time to do that kind of an in-depth study of the Forget Commission report and the UI Program. I suspect that he was listening to the nattering nabobs in the bureaucracy. In fact, I have absolutely no doubt about it. He was listening to those who are determined to maintain the status quo, those who feel that the only good ideas come from the bureaucracy.
We expected something different from this Government. After all, that is why we changed the parliamentary rules dealing with committees. The Government could have had its way in the committee. The whips could have been put on in

May 19, 1987
Supply
committee, but they were not. To the credit of the Conservative members of the committee, they recognized that what we proposed was fair and just.
I compared what the committee proposed to what Forget proposed. There are similarities in 22 areas. The Minister could have moved in 22 areas. There would have been a considerable positive improvement in the Unemployment Insurance Program if the Government had moved in those 22 areas.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-UI REFORM-FULL EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Why didn't it?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-UI REFORM-FULL EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
That is a good question and I will deal with it, but I want to set the stage first.
The Minister is now saying that he did not want to rile up the people on the right or the people of the left. It reminds me of the story of a Minister of Employment and Immigration who got lost in the maze of the UI system. As night was falling, he saw a light shining. As he moved toward this light, he saw that it came from a little cottage in the maze. He went in and saw that there were three bowls of porridge on the table. He took a little sip from the first one and he said: "Oh, that's too cold". Then he took a sip from the second bowl and he said: "Oh, that's too hot". Then he came to the third one, he sipped from it and he said: "Oh, just right, just where I want to be, up on a fence getting splinters". That is the position the Minister took on the Ul Program.
I want the Minister to know that the UI Program is not a fairy-tale. The unemployed do not want the Minister to use fairy-tales to solve the problems they face.
For example, the Minister could have moved on maternity benefits. The committee proposed and Forget supported the elimination of the waiting period for maternity benefits. The cost to the UI Program would be $60 million. We proposed and Forget agreed that we have to use UI benefits that the unemployed have collected to help with training programs and to start new businesses because the people who are unemployed could in many cases create their own jobs. We proposed that they should be able to draw on their benefits at the back end of the program in order to be able to go where there may be a job. We proposed reforms of the administration.
For example, there are 214 vice-presidents at the very top to run the unemployment insurance program. Their total cost to the UI program is $15 million. We argued for more services on line to help the unemployed. We recognize that the Unemployment Insurance Program is generating a surplus. Last year it generated $800 million and this year it is expected to generate a surplus of $1.7 million. All of that is to pay off the deficit created by the recession of 1982.
We say that $450 million would have been the cost of putting into effect the proposals of the standing committee. Had they put in place only the 22 areas which were agreed upon, it would have cost less than $450 million. We could have
created equity, flexibility and simplicity in the Unemployment Insurance Program. God knows that the unemployed right across the country and those who represent them have been crying to the Government to improve the Unemployment Insurance Program.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-UI REFORM-FULL EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was surprised when, in his opening remarks, my good friend, the Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez), suggested that the Liberal Party may not be sincere in opting for a full unemployment policy. Is the Hon. Member not aware that following the Second World War the Liberal Party, under Mackenzie King, opted for a full employment policy and in fact maintained employment at an average of 3 per cent for seven years? When Mike Pearson came to power in 1963, the Liberal Party again opted for a full employment policy and maintained an average of between 3 and 4 per cent unemployment for three years.
I know that from 1977 to 1984 that was not our highest priority. I admit that we in the Party make mistakes from time to time. However, since it was done before in this country, does the Member not think it is possible to do it again, especially when we look at the examples of Sweden, Japan, Austria and Switzerland? All of those countries have adopted full employment policies in recent years and have been able to achieve more or less full employment. If they can do it in those countries and if we did it before in Canada, can we not do it again?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-UI REFORM-FULL EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank my hon. friend for the question. It is interesting that he chose the period right after the Second World War and the period of the Pearson era of 1962. The answer to that is very simple. In the first case, the CCF was breathing down the neck of the minority Mackenzie King Government. During the Mike Pearson era, the NDP was breathing down the necks of the Liberals. There is nothing like a minority government to concentrate the minds of Liberals on full employment. In contrast, every time they have a majority government, that is forgotten. That is very unfortunate. I propose that the Hon. Member read our document, Canada Unlimited, which lays out the New Democratic Party's strategy for creating full employment.
During most of the years that I have been in Canada I have experienced Liberal rule. I have lived in northern Ontario and have seen a resource economy devastated by unemployment. I have never seen any kind of economic strategy, regional, provincial or national, put in place which would allow the resources of Canada to be refined where they are produced. Falconbridge still ships raw nickel to Norway to be refined and the finished product is sold back to Canada. Hardwood pulp from Nackawick, New Brunswick, is still shipped to Belgium where it is refined into photographic paper and then shipped back here. That is where the jobs are.
I remember Tommy Douglas preaching when I joined this Party that we are nothing but hewers of wood and drawers of water. The Minister has now proposed free trade as the panacea to create employment. We have free trade in the
May 19, 1987

nickel industry. Our nickel crosses the United States border without any duty being paid, but I have seen no investment in northern Ontario in the equipment which goes underground to mine.
One would think that we would be the centre of manufacturing of mining equipment. One would think that the North would be the centre of research and development in new mining techniques. That is not the case, Mr. Speaker. That is all done abroad in Virginia in the United States, in England and in Europe. We do not even produce the technology here for the things that we do well such as mining. I know how my western colleagues feel about eastern Canada because we feel the same way about Toronto. Even the iron ore which is taken out of northern Ontario is shipped south for refining.
We in the NDP are committed to full employment and have policies which bind our Party to establishing an environment in which we can have full employment. It is an achievable goal which has been reached in other countries where social democratic Governments are in power. When we have been in government in this country we have worked toward full employment and have achieved it.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-UI REFORM-FULL EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I know the Hon. Member is a fair person and would not want to mislead the House. It is true that in 1963 Mike Pearson had a minority Government, but there certainly were not minority Governments in 1948 or 1952 when Mackenzie King and Louis St. Laurent were Prime Ministers. I admit that in the 1944 election the CCF fought a valiant battle and elected a large number of Members to this House, so what he said is partly true.
I am pleased that the Member's Party has such an elaborate policy for full employment, because we know that after the next election he will be able to support our Party in putting a full employment policy into effect.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-UI REFORM-FULL EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was in this House when my Party did that once before. At that time I swore that I would never let it happen again. I am hoping that it will not get to that. The way things are going these days there may be several baby Liberal Parties rather than one Liberal Party running in the next election. However, that is in the future and I do not want to deal with the future or with the past which my hon. friend has put forward.
Everyone who has studied the Unemployment Insurance Program has said that unemployment is not the problem- employment is the problem. Beyond that the positions are all over the place. The Minister and the Government seem to accept that you cannot achieve full employment in this country.
I have 26 municipalities in my constituency. The sewer systems, roads, and water systems need to be refurbished and we have the people to do the work. However, these municipalities do not have a sufficient corporate tax base to raise the money to spend on those refurbishings. If this were to be done, the cost would rest very heavily on the home owner. We do not
Supply
have the corporate tax base, which means the home owner would be overtaxed in order to do this essential refurbishing.
The mayors of this great country presented a brief to the Government in which they asked it to establish a municipal fund. Over a period of five to ten years some millions of dollars could be spent refurbishing the communities and their infrastructures. In the long run, this is very essential to the attraction of entrepreneurial endeavours, and I suggest that this is a direction in which we should be moving because it makes common sense.
If the Government is sincere about defeating the scourge of unemployment and can find a billion dollars to bail out the depositors of two banks, why can it not find the money to invest, not only to improve the quality of life in the communities, but to provide gainful employment and maintain the dignity of people while doing so?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-UI REFORM-FULL EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Resuming debate, the Hon. Member for Richmond-Wolfe (Mr. Tardif).

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-UI REFORM-FULL EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I also welcome this opportunity to express my views on the motion put forward by my colleague, and I would like to quote it for discussion's sake, if you allow me, Mr. Speaker:
That this House condemn the Government for its failure to initiate meaningful reform in the unemployment insurance system and for its failure to commit itself to a full employment policy that seriously addresses high regional unemployment, youth unemployment, part-time work and labour market adjustment.
Mr. Speaker, I am especially pleased to have an opportunity to speak on that important matter. I would like if I may, for the purposes of discussion, to refer to the days following September 4, 1984 when faced with the important issue of unemployment which affected thousands of Canadians, the Government said it was aware, it was concerned, it was conscious of the thousands of problems it faced with unemployment insurance. Faced with that real problem, that real evil, the Government told us during the first months of its administration: We will strive for reconciliation, communication-ours will be a policy of analysis and consultation. It was trumpeted there would indeed be major consultation initiatives, also major pauses for thought.
It must also be understood that while those pauses for hesitation, reflection and analysis were going on, they had the Forget Commission travelling across Canada to hear representations from all those who were concerned with the important matter of unemployment. Each time the Opposition tried to know what would be the Government's position in that strategic area, we were told: Look here, we will make no decisions, if only out of respect for the Commission who is now sitting, we will wait for the Commission's report.
We were also told at the time, Mr. Speaker, that Parliament's work should be enhanced, committees should

May 19, 1987
Supply
regain prestige and in some way credibility, they should also be involved in the redirection process, the process of suggesting to Government measures needed by the country. Of course, since then, the Forget Commission has tabled its report. Also, a committee of the House has spent months studying very seriously and thoroughly the whole question of unemployment in Canada and has tabled recommendations just as the Forget Commission did. And following those two exercises of very great significance and value, in my view, what is the answer of the government? The status quo.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that this is another proof of the almost complete and widespread carelessness of this government. The government had there, I think, an opportunity to propose to Canadian men and women an alternative- admittedly not a panacea-but an approach, a new direction that constitute a real improvement compared to the current situation. But the government has chosen to continue with the status quo, ignoring naturally the important issue of youth unemployment, ignoring the important issue of unemployment among part time workers, ignoring or rather simply dismissing the dramatic problems facing remote regions. The Government said: Even though we are always blaming and criticizing the former Government, let us continue exactly as before. That is why the House is being asked to maintain just about the same system.
I suggest that in view of the circumstances, the motion moved by my hon. friend is quite in order and that this decidedly scandalous decision demonstrates that the Government does not give a hoot about all these men and women who have worked for months and years to put together valid proposals. In its arrogant and insensitive attitude, it demonstrates that it could not care less for all these proposals and suggestions, which I feel were quite reasonable and equitable and which simply had to be put forward.
Mr. Speaker, I represent in the House of Commons a riding which is partly rural, which depends to a very large extent on regional development policies, and which has been very seriously affected by various problems these past few years. A lot of my constituents were economically dependent on the production of asbestos which, as you know, has had to be curtailed, and is still going through an incredibly difficult period, so much so that workers by the thousands have lost their jobs, and very well paid ones at that. This industry plays a major role in the economy of my riding.
An other issue with tremendous economic impact within my riding is that of the footwear industry. My riding depends very heavily on the footwear industry. Well, the Government announced over a year ago the total elimination of quotas, implying that it would take steps to compensate for these thousands of jobs which were automatically lost because of its decision.
Such is the situation of two major industries in my riding, and it is not unique in Canada. There are many other such
ridings dependent upon sectors like asbestos mining and the shoe industry, which were really counting on a new direction and new provisions to get a glimmer of hope that they could overcome the difficulties they had been facing, in many cases for several years. What response is the government giving those thousands of workers? Things will remain exactly as they are now.
Mr. Speaker, the main town of my riding is Asbestos, a community of about 13,000 people six or seven years ago, which now has only 6,500 or 6,700 people. Workers in Asbestos had bought a house, they were homeowners with a decent income, earning enough to live comfortably. Most of those workers were aged between 35 and 45. They had worked all their life for a concern called Johns-Manville, an asbestos producing corporation. These people, who had no special training, who had not had to change jobs, who had not much experience outside the specific sector of an asbestos mine, lost their jobs because of a stagnant market due to decreasing consumer demand and decreasing production. Of course, UI provisions allowed them to get unemployment benefits after a certain waiting period. But in order to find another job, they had to be able to take advantage of what could be called transitional measures or training courses not only to become aware of the market opportunities, but also to gain the qualifications necessary to fill a second or third job. What is the Government's answer to that? Nothing.
Mr. Speaker, the problem is the same in the case of the shoe industry although it might have been a bit more dramatic, because workers in this industry are, in many cases, relatively older and extremely difficult to retrain. In the absence of training or retraining courses, these people have, in effect, no chance whatsoever of finding another job.
Mr. Speaker, to all these workers, we said: You do not have any chance with the federal Government. Do whatever you want. We are throwing in the towel. We do not have anything to offer you that can make you more optimistic about the future.
It was a real opportunity, a great chance for this Government to regain its credibility in terms of the regions and to prove that they are important. Once again, I think that the regions have no importance whatsoever for a Conservative Government and that the Tories try, by all means, to put all their eggs in one basket to the detriment of the large regions, including the one I represent.
The Governement also had, Mr. Speaker-and I think that this is clear enough in the many recommendations-the opportunity to modify, to simplify, the provisions relating to the Unemployment Insurance Act, to make them more consistent, if I may say so. In the last few years, I have had to represent dozens, if not hundreds of beneficiaries, people who lost their jobs and who had a number of problems when the time came to collect their benefits. I therefore had several dozens of occasions to represent and defend them in front of the arbitration board, so that they could receive what I consider, in many cases, to be barely a fair amount.
May 19, 1987

One need not have experienced the arbitration process very often, Mr. Speaker, to realize what a mess it is. I am not questioning the competence of those nominated to arbitration boards. Quite to the contrary, these people do their best to simplify and to humanize the Unemployment Insurance Act and its regulations. But it is all so complicated that one often gets the impression that these well intentioned and extremely competent people get lost in the maze and do not really know what to base their decisions on. We had a unique opportunity to simplify all this legislation and all these regulations to make them into one coherent and accessible body so that once and for all it would have been within the grasp of the average person to understand what one was entitled to or not.
Mr. Speaker, in a rural or semi-rural riding like the one I represent, I would venture to say that 80 per cent of the constituents we meet wish to bring to our attention problems which have to do with unemployment insurance.
As far as I am concerned, I do not think that it is exaggerated to say that eight cases out of 10 have to do with unemployment insurance. And after eight years as the Member for Richmond-Wolfe, it has become unequivocally obvious to me that those who come to my office are generally upstanding breadwinners who are at fault or have lost their job. It is usually their first or second experience with unemployment insurance and unfortunately, in the vast majority of cases, they are innocent victims. By that I meant to say that those who are used to bridging the gap or who have had the opportunity to collect unemployment insurance on 10, 15 or 20 occasions finally manage to understand the system to some degree and to act accordingly.
But, Mr. Speaker, particularly in a riding such as mine, where many people are new entrants looking for a job for the first or the second time, they might experience problems with unemployment insurance services and they can't figure out why. And regrettably, there is also an unpleasant attitude on the part of unemployment office personnel, which can be explained by the fact that they probably see more people in a single day than any other government office, but there the people looking for jobs have the feeling they are just numbers, nobodies, being treated in a very callous and inconsiderate manner, without any kind of consideration althought they are up against administrative problems or perhaps just a lack of understanding. So it seems to me that it would not have been presumptuous to expect to see a more accessible, more sensible and more coherent system thus allowing the people facing problems with the Unemployment Insurance Commission to quickly know their entitlement to benefits. Instead of that, the Government has chosen to perpetuate the complexity, the confusion, to keep the "monster" alive. Mr. Speaker, for the area I represent, which is far away in many respects from the larger centers, there seems to be within the recommendations some sort of major and real improvement which is summarized in the first recommendation where it is said that we should adopt a standard entrance requirement of ten weeks of
Supply
insurable employment. Taken out of context, that recommendation per se may seem a bit generous, even questionnable. However, in context, this recommendation illustrates quite well how with such a simple measure we could have solved dozens of problems.
My riding is in the immediate vicinity of what is known as the queen of the Eastern Townships, the City of Sherbrooke. Recent statistics showed the economic recovery in that community to be one the most dynamic in Canada. It is from this buoyant, job creating community of Sherbrooke, with over
150,000	residents that the economic situation is assessed and statistics prepared. My riding which, as I said, is located in the immediate vicinity of Sherbrooke, is an indirect victim of this prosperity in the sense that, to determine entrance requirements to qualify for unemployment insurance benefits, the statistics concerning Sherbrooke totally misrepresent the whole situation to the point that, in Asbestos and surrounding areas, the rate of unemployemnt is actually in the order of 35 per cent, and even 38, 39 and 40 per cent. At some 60 or 70 miles from Asbestos, the rate of unemployment is much or rather substantially lower, which directly contributes, you will agree with me, Mr. Speaker, to penalizing heavily all of those earning their living from, and depending on the activities related to asbestos, textiles and shoe manufacturing.
I will conclude, Mr. Speaker, by saying that, after all the time taken by the Government to supposedly ponder the matter and fully understand the situation, it was quite a disappointment to see it come up with such an appalling and callous decision for all those men and women hoping for a new direction. I do hope that next polls will once again make the Government realize it is totally off the track and that, unless it comes to its senses, it might not survive the next election.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was looking forward to making a speech this afternoon but I guess that we will soon run out of time. It is almost as if the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand) has been filling in the question and comment period to the point that it is now impossible in terms of time to make a speech.
I sat here throughout the day listening to members of the Opposition, including the Hon. Member who has just spoken, bemoan the fact that Canada does not yet have full employment. Over the past two and a half years I cannot think of a single exception to the following rule. Every time the Government proposes something that is good for the economy and good for job creation it is opposed by members of the Opposition. In this regard I wrote down a short list while listening to other Hon. Members speak. The list is as follows: the Patent Act, free trade, tax reform, transportation reform, agricultural war and what we are doing about it, reducing the deficit, getting rid of the National Energy Program, changing FIR A to Investment Canada, and the selling of Dome to a company which has some money and which can create some activity.

May 19, 1987
Supply
Every single one of those initiatives created jobs in the country. Every single one is being fought by members of both opposition Parties. It is a bit hypocritical to have to listen to a debate wherein Members opposite challenge the Government for its record in terms of full employment and then turn around day after day and fight everything that can produce jobs for Canadians. It is time to call a spade a spade and to make the point that I have made.
In terms of unemployment insurance, it is an astounding phenomenon to me as chairman of the committee which reported to the House on March 19 the degree to which business had a knee-jerk reaction to its report. I think it is fair to say that every single national business organization in the country condemned the report of the standing committee. Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to take part today in this debate on the motion tabled by my colleague in the opposition, the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand), regarding the reform of unemployment insurance.
I wanted to take part in this debate because the Hon. Member worked with us on the report of the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration concerning unemployment insurance.
Supply
Mr. Speaker, what is the Hon. Member of the Official Opposition proposing in his motion? He says:
That this House condemn the Government for its failure to initiate meaningful
reform in the unemployment insurance system and for its failure to commit
itself to a full employment, youth unemployment, part-time work and labour
market adjustement.
That is the motion from the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East. He is condemning the Government for failing to initiate meaningful reform in the unemployement insurance system. Really, Mr. Speaker, what I perceive in this motion is some frustration on the part of the Hon. Member. He is frustrated because the recommandations contained in the report of the standing committee have not been accepted entirely by the Government.
I understand why the Hon. Member is unhappy to see that all of our recommendations have not been accepted by the Government. I too, Mr. Speaker, worked on that committee. We each have spent may be a hundred hours studying the Forget Report and the minority opinions. We have met with some 50 groups of witnesses. We fought each other to have our views accepted by the standing committee, or to have them endorsed in a consensus. And above all, members of the three Parties, New Democrats, Liberals and Tory Government members, attempted together and succeeded in reaching a consensus on 89 of the 90 recommendations of the Hawkes Report.
That was some achievement, Mr. Speaker. We could have done what the Forget Commission did and submitted three reports to the Government: one report for the New Democratic Party, one for the Liberal Party, and one for the Government Party, the Conservative Party. And even possibly individual reports too. We could have done that, Mr. Speaker. It would have been quite different. But no, Mr. Speaker, we managed to reach an agreement and a consensus on 89 of the 90 recommendations.
The Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East is disappointed and frustrated to see that our work was not acknowledged. However, Mr. Speaker, I believe that the Hon. Member should instead be proud and satisfied to see that a major recommendation of our report, the standing committee report, the Hawkes Report, was acknowledged and accepted by the Government. Yes, Mr. Speaker, there was a recommendation or a kind of preamble in our report which said that our committee opposed in the strongest terms the implementation of the annualization formula of the Forget Commission.
It was an extremely important suggestion, Mr. Speaker, and it was accepted by the Government. The viewpoint of the standing committee on that matter was upheld.
With respect to the Government accepting our point of view in the report, I think that the annualization formula was in itself worth all our efforts in the standing committee, because the annualization formula meant for all practical purposes that unemployment insurance benefits were to be cut in half.

May 19, 1987
Supply
What the Forget Commission advocated, Mr. Speaker, was that the income of claimants should be determined on an annual basis. Let us take for instance a worker who earns $400 per week and works for a period of 26 weeks because he is seasonally employed. The unemployment benefit payments to that worker after that period of 26 weeks at work would normally amount to 60 per cent of his income, or $240 per week. With the annualization formula presented by the Forget Commission, we would have brought the amount of $400 a week on an annual basis, which would have meant that the person would have earned $200 a week since it would have been on an annual basis. Sixty per cent of $200 a week equals $120. You see the difference for those who are unfortunately on unemployment insurance. Instead of having $240 as before, they would have seen their income fall to $120.
Accepting the annualization formula would have had disastrous effects in some areas, namely in those which have a strong touristic potential. It would have had serious consequences for seasonal workers, fishermen, etc. Moreover, it would have transferred the bill to the provinces. This is why, as members of the standing committee, we must be pleased that this recommendation was rejected, as recommended by our committee.
Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, I would like to remind my colleagues and more particularly the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand) that the positions of business people and of unions were completely opposed. They were even polarized in the debate. On the one hand, business people were looking favourably at the Forget Commission Report, but it was not the case for the unions which simply rejected it. As far as the report of our standing committee is concerned, positions were simply reversed, Mr. Speaker. What could we do then? Accept the first report and reject the second one? Or accept the second report and reject the first? There is something worse than an imperfect status quo on unemployment insurance, namely to make a reform leading to social chaos.
However I agree with my colleague, particularly, as a Member from a region with a high unemployment rate, that some job creating proposals should have been implemented concerning, for instance, work sharing and lump sum payments to claimants wishing to start a business. I was hoping for that kind of recommendation, Mr. Speaker, but I still hope that some of them will be implemented at a more appropriate time.
As I was saying earlier we have reached a consensus on 89 of the 90 recommendations of the standing committee's report. Mr. Speaker I am the one who broke the consensus on one of them, recommendation No. 17, which stated:
That pension income not be treated as earned salary during a benefit period.
It meant that we had to go back to the situation prevailing two years ago when pension income was not considered as an income for unemployment insurance purposes. Mr. Speaker, we know perfectly well that this Government will not accept it, so why should we give false hopes to early retirees? I refused
to accept it because the new pension policy had been implemented since January 1986 and had already created problems because those who had gone into early retirement had "misinterpreted" the rules. Workers who retired before January 5, 1986 thought that they would be entitled to unemployment insurance for a year, and rightly so. And Mr. Speaker, we should have gone back a year and a half. What were the people supposed to do from January 5, 1986 until the adoption of the new legislation? Can you imagine the confusion it would have created among early retirees when all this had been clearly announced and all Canadians are aware, since January 5, 1986, that pension income is considered as income?
So, I opposed this recommendation because I refuse to create false expectations. It is not true that I could be made to vote in committee for something contrary to my conscience and which would create false expectations.
Going back to the Opposition motion, Mr. Speaker, that motion implies that this Government has no full employment policy, that it does not seem to contemplate any action in that direction. 1 suggest that a few statistics are in order if we are to adopt the proper perspective. Since our election on September 1984, we have created 778,000 jobs in Canada according to figures and more than 80 per cent of those jobs were full time employment compared with a reverse 80 per cent parttime jobs for the previous Government. Of those 778 000 jobs, 427 000 were for women. The national unemployment rate decreased from 11.7 per cent to 9.3 per cent. There is still work to be done of course. But we are fully aware of it and we will keep on working to achieve full employment.
As far as young people are concerned, as recently as yesterday, I received in my office a 22-year-old young man who came to see me for a job. He is one of those persons who have problems finding their way into the labour market. It is never easy meeting with unemployed in search of the job they want to regain their self-esteem and achieve their full potential in our society. I will spare you the details about that young man. Yesterday, for instance, I saw a 22 year old who had finished Grade 11. When we look at the employment opportunities in regions like ours, when companies like Alcan, Abitibi-Price and Cascade are no longer hiring but introducing new technology and reducing the number of jobs, it is definitely something to be concerned about. We have to start asking ourselves what kind of focus we want to give our regional economy so these young people can develop their potential and get the jobs to which they are entitled. And that is why I still believe in the concept of job sharing, something for which I fought as a member of the standing committee. What good does it do to work 40 hours a week when the Government takes our taxes to pay some unfortunate who has to stay home and who would much rather have a job and develop his own potential? I think our big corporations will have to take this step some day. Why not take advantage of the situation to improve the lives of Canadians and give young people and older workers who lose their jobs because of technological
May 19, 1987

change a chance to have the jobs they need to support their families and continue to develop their potential in our society.
Mr. Speaker, to get back to the figures, we have created
778,000	jobs, and I repeat, the unemployment rate is 9.3 per cent. So there is still a lot to be done, and that is why we need the Opposition's help to get the unemployment rate down even further, but not systematic opposition to our proposals. I wonder how much time Opposition Members have made us waste in some committees, voicing objections as a matter of principle. That is what happens, and that is when reforming the standing committees becomes important, Mr. Speaker.
We have been told we have no comprehensive policy. I beg to differ. Unlike the previous Government, we have dispensed with the shortsighted policy that consists in creating short term jobs. Our predecessors' only concern was the unemployment rate in the here and now. They ignored the structural and cyclical aspects of the economy and the specific needs of the various regions in this country. Mr. Speaker, I heard one of our Members referring earlier to Toronto, where the need for unemployment insurance was not that great.
I may remind Hon. Members that Canada is more than just cities like Toronto. There are regions like the Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean where the unemployment rate is not 4 or 5 per cent but 12 and 14 per cent, most of the time. In Toronto there may be some newspapers that have employment sections 30 pages long, which is not the case in the Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean. We have to consider the situation across this country. And across this country, there are regions that are disadvantaged. There is regional disparity, and we must take that into account.
This Government has dropped the concept of short term measures and opted for a long term policy. Long term employment means employment that requires adequate preparation and training that is relevant to the job. Hence our jobs strategy program.
For the first time, our country has a national policy based on a consensus of social and economic experts and involving specific goals to ensure that specific clients are provided with the skills required for their involvement in the labour market. Mr. Speaker, I am not going to take up too much time dealing with those objectives. Let me just deal with one of them.
The Canadian Jobs Strategy meets the needs of people who are most in need of a job. It is an innovative strategy which recognizes the fundamental relationship which should exist between training and employment creation. Its goal is to give people who need it most the means to find their way into the labour market, on the occasion of their first experience of the labour market or when they are forced to train into another job or to take a new direction in their career.
Mr. Speaker, here are those client groups. Young people, young men and women who have difficulties finding their way into the labour market, because of the usual Catch 22: no job without experience, no experience without a job; women who wish to become gainfully employed after being away from the
Supply
labour market for a long time; workers whose employment is threatened by the evolution of technologies or of markets; workers in communities affected by an economic slowdown when there are signs of a possible recovery; and students who need to earn money to complete their education, and I think our Challenge Program speaks for itself in this respect: $180 million this year for the Student Employment Program. And every year, Mr. Speaker, we reject requests by companies and private businesses, non-profit organizations and others. Many more requests than we can cater for. That is an indication that the program is efficient and effective. Finally, people whose professional activity may improve the workings of the labour market.
During the last financial year, actions taken under the Canadian Jobs Strategy have resulted in the involvement of over 450,000 people, or 5 per cent of our labour market. That is an achievement which would not even have been dreamed of by the Government of which the sponsor of the motion before us today was a Member.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I shall not vote for the motion introduced by the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace- Lachine East (Mr. Allmand). I would only like to say that if the Opposition showed the least interest in the Canadian people, it would not introduce this kind of motion and would co-operate with the present Government to bring about some improvements to the programs already in place and whatever measures we intend to introduce for the Canadian people.

I would like to emphasize the importance of this issue, and perhaps a good way of doing that would be to refer to a Canadian film I saw the other night, John and the Missus, starring Gordon Pinsent. Members had a chance to see that film, they would feel something of the hurt that individuals, families and whole communities feel when a single-industry town is destroyed.

insurance and other years he did not. Whether he was able to collect unemployment insurance or not made all the difference to our family's Christmas and to our standard of living. The importance of unemployment insurance to many families in many communities cannot be underestimated. That is particularly the case for seasonal workers.
It is sometimes easy for people who have never missed a pay cheque to think that seasonal workers with their dependence upon the unemployment insurance system are ripping the system off. Yet the basic primary industries on which the Canadian economy depends, forestry, fishing, construction and agriculture, are all industries that are to a large extent seasonal. Yet these are the very people who were the major target of the Forget Commission's recommendation that there be a system of annualization which would reduce the benefits these people bring home. The elimination of regional benefits and the phasing out of benefits for fishermen and their families would affect seasonal workers, the people who were targeted by the Forget Commission.

As my colleague, the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez), has pointed out, some 22 of the 90 recommendations of the standing committee were right in line with the Forget Commission recommendations. Yet the Government refused to deal with them. These recommendations would have helped deal with unemployed workers who need further training or want some help starting small businesses.
1 and many other Members have had many unemployed workers come to us with a great desire to use their time of unemployment in a constructive way. They want to further their education or perhaps to start small businesses. They do not simply want to be on the dole. Yet the present restrictive unemployment insurance policy does not allow them to use their time constructively. Our recommendations would have allowed for that, but the Government chose not to act on them.
The Government did not act on the recommendation for some kind of assistance for older workers. Again, certainly in my constituency and in many other parts of Canada which are dependent upon single-resource industries where those resources are in trouble, there are many older workers who need desperately some kind of additional assistance over and above that which the present program provides. The Government has chosen not to act there.
The Government could have eliminated the waiting period for maternity benefits. On a number of areas on which there was consensus, the Government has chosen not to act. We must ask why this is so.
In the minute I have left, I would like to emphasize that the primary problem is not with the Unemployment Insurance Program but with the lack of jobs in Canada. The Government is not addressing that problem in the way it should. It has cut back on regional programs, on job-creation programs and on several Departments. For example, it is refusing to fund adequately the small craft harbours to maintain infrastructure for fishermen and tourism and to provide jobs. Small craft harbours will be closed down because of the programs of this Government which refuses to see the need to maintain basic infrastructures and keep basic jobs for a vibrant economy. I lay that upon the Government. I ask it to take a second look at the recommendations of the standing committee and bring in a UI proposal which will be responsive to the real needs of the Canadian people.
