subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-REQUEST FOR LISTING OF HONORARY BALTIC CONSULS
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-REQUEST FOR LISTING OF HONORARY BALTIC CONSULS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 1 I directed a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) with regard to the listing of honorary Baltic consuls in the External Affairs directory of diplomatic, consular and other representatives in Canada. The Minister responded that the question was under review by his Department.
This matter has been in limbo since 1972 and clearly should have long since been resolved. For 10 years prior to 1972 the consuls were listed in the directory and it was only on the death of the acting Honorary Consul General of Estonia that year that the listing of the consuls were removed from the directory.
The federal Government has received countless representations from the Estonian Central Council in Canada, the Latvian Federation in Canada, the Lithuanian Canadian Community, the Captive Nations Committee in Canada and the Baltic Federation, yet their efforts have produced no results. Despite Canada's de jure nonrecognition of the illegal occupation of the Baltic states of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania by the Soviet Union, the Baltic consuls are still not listed as the representatives of the pre-Soviet occupation, freely and democratically elected governments of the Baltic States.
Over the years there have been many answers given as to who is responsible for the listings. On different occasions the Baltic communities have been informed that the listing is at the discretion of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, that the responsibility lies with the Parliament of Canada in persuading the Secretary of State for External Affairs to list the Baltic consuls, that the question of listing of Baltic consuls must be decided by the Cabinet, and that the question of listing the Baltic consuls should be decided by the inner Cabinet.
With all these conflicting responses, it is small wonder that the Baltic communities are left confused and concerned as to how this matter can be resolved when it cannot even be established who is responsible. In the past, two Secretaries of State for External Affairs have commissioned reports to study the issue, neither of which were ever made public. The Minister's assurance that the issue is under review can therefore be of little comfort to the Baltic communities.
In discussions with representatives of the Department of External Affairs, representatives have been told that the listings would have a negative effect on "other areas". Such statements have led to the conclusion that the Department of
May 19, 1987

External Affairs is concerned that the listing of consuls would anger the Soviet Union and, consequently, allows that fear to determine our policy on this important matter.
There are those in our Department of External Affairs who advocate that Canada should not do anything to ruffle the feathers of the U.S.S.R. They always recommend the path of least resistance and are proverbial fence-sitters. Such a position is an abrogation and betrayal of our principles as a free and democratic sovereign nation. For us to appease a morally bankrupt Soviet regime, whose only trumps are a mighty military apparatus, an aggressive stance toward the rest of the world, and their traditionally arrogant rhetoric, would constitute a betrayal of all those who gave their lives for freedom and democracy, all those who came to this country believing that Canada was a country which stands for fundamental freedom and human rights, including respect of territorial integrity and the right of self-determination.
If Canada continues to sit on the fence by refusing to list Baltic consuls, the Soviets will tell the people of the Baltic States that while Canada pays lip service to the principle of withholding de jure recognition of the captivity of their countries, in practice Canada has conceded Soviet sovereignty and Soviet right to enforce its illegal annexation. This is a discredit to our entire system of government.
The United States already accords the Baltic consuls full diplomatic recognition. It has led the way, and Australia has followed its lead by recognizing the honorary consul of the Latvian consulate.
The time for Canada to act is now. I urge Canada to stand up and be counted. I urge the Minister to list the Baltic consuls in the External Affairs directory of diplomatic, consular, and other representatives in Canada. In doing so, we demonstrate our continuing commitment to the principles and purpose of the United Nations Charter and to the cause of peace and freedom in the world. By our action, we will be sending out a message to oppressive regimes throughout the world that our principles are not and will not be for sale.
Given that the issue of listing Baltic consuls has already undergone at least two previous reviews, and in light of the decision by Australia to accord recognition to the honorary consul for Latvia, will the Minister now agree to take advantage of the opportunity to once and for all put an end to continuous studies on this matter and restore the listing of the Baltic consuls?

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Guy Hudon (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-REQUEST FOR LISTING OF HONORARY BALTIC CONSULS
speechtext:
On behalf of the Government, Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to state Canada's policy with respect to the Baltic States, namely Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania. Every Canadian Government since 1940 has firmly refused to give de jure recognition to the forced annexation of these countries by the U.S.S.R. However Canada does give de
Adjournment Debate
facto recognition to their incorporation into the Soviet Union since the latter country exercises authority. The refusal of Canada to give de jure recognition to the annexation of the Baltic States goes far beyond mere words and includes measures which underscore the special status of the Baltic States as independent nations illegally annexed by the U.S.S.R. during World War II.
The Government allows the acting honorary consuls of the Baltic States to continue exercising their duties in Canada, although it does not formaly recognize them since honorary consuls are not appointed by a government with which Canada maintains diplomatic or consular relations. These consuls are Canadian citizens and for this reason have no immunity nor diplomatic privileges. Canadian ambassadors do not travel in the Baltic States.
As much as possible, other Canadian officials who do travel there avoid all contacts with local authorities. For purposes of Canadian passport and immigration documents, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania remain acceptable as references for places of birth. Since Baltic passports do not guarantee reentry into Baltic countries, Canadian legislation does not consider them acceptable for admission to Canada. This is why extraordinary procedures have been adopted to clear the way for admission to Canada of Baltic representatives of other countries who come here in the discharge of their duties. These measures prove that Canada continues to reject the legality of Soviet control over Baltic countries, a fact which Soviet authorities have duly noted. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) has already advised the House that he is reviewing the question of adding the names of Baltic acting honorary consuls in the publication of the Department of External Affairs entitled "Diplomatic Corps and Consular and Other Representatives in Canada". The Minister is fully aware of the views expressed in this respect by the Baltic community in Canada; he will give particular consideration to them and to the general implications of such a decision for Canada's foreign policy.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I can assure the House that the Government of Canada does not intend to change this policy under which it does not give de jure recognition to the Soviet annexation of the Baltic States.

subtopic: CANADIAN HUMAN RIGHTS COMMISSION-APPOINTMENT OF ANTONIO ARCANGEL TO HUMAN RIGHTS COMMISSION. REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION OF APPOINTEE
CANADIAN HUMAN RIGHTS COMMISSION-APPOINTMENT OF ANTONIO ARCANGEL TO HUMAN RIGHTS COMMISSION. REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION OF APPOINTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am rising to object to the Government's cavalier and callous appointment of those people who would represent our country on the Canadian Human Rights Tribunal.
The House will recall that my specific question related to the case of one Antonio Arcangel who was appointed by the Government to sit on the Canadian Human Rights Tribunal, even though he had given a public interview in which he supported the long-term imposition of martial law in the

May 19, 1987
Adjournment Debate
Philippines. He basically suggested that life in the Philippines was good during the tenure of Ferdinand and Imelda Marcos but had deteriorated since the arrival of Corazon Aquino.
As a result of my intervention in the House, the appointee subsequently withdrew from consideration but, at the same time, we witnessed the ridiculous situation of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) suggesting to the House that it was the fault of the Opposition or, in some way, my fault because I had brought the facts surrounding Mr. Arcangel's appointment to the attention of the public via the Question Period process.
We see today a second appointee, another one of these rather questionable Conservative appointments to the Canadian Human Rights Tribunal in the form of an appointee in the Yukon who gave an interview in the local press, making some comments suggesting that the native community was living at the expense of other taxpayers for the last number of years. When this question was raised in the House today and in committee, the Minister not only refused to expedite the investigation, but proceeded to suggest that it was perhaps all right in the interim because this particular individual might not be appointed to hear a human rights case.
As a result of the Arcangel case and subsequent cases which have been repeatedly brought to the attention of the Minister, who seems bent on appointing Tory hacks who have no interest in human rights and who in fact have shown to our committee that they not only are not interested in human rights but do not even understand the basic question of equality, the Minister should come forward with some specific recommendations to ensure that people who are appointed by this Government, or any government, to rule on matters of a quasi judicial nature-which is what we see in terms of human rights rulings-have a demonstrated competence in the area of human rights. The Minister should also be prepared to act quickly and expeditiously when problems are brought to his attention.
The Minister in the past has doctored resumes, removing, for example, in the case of Progressive Conservative appointees, any reference to their affiliation to the Conservative Party. Through his own Department, he has been involved with or condoned meetings which were set up in the Privy Council Office to brief appointees so that they knew exactly how to respond to members of the committee. Further, when matters such as the case of Flo Whyard in the Yukon are brought to his attention, as it was by letter more than a month ago, the Minister seems unprepared to act.
It seems a shame that Members of this House, either through Question Period or through committee, have to repeatedly bring to the attention of the Minister and the Government individual cases of concern with respect to human rights appointees. Quite clearly, it is the responsibility of the Minister and the Government to ensure that an objective
process is put in place to ensure quality appointees to the Human Rights Tribunal.
That was not the case in the Arcangel situation. Certainly the Minister has dragged his heels with respect to concerns raised about the statements made in a newspaper article entitled "The Problem of Handouts", which was actually written by a human rights appointee. The so-called investigation the Minister plans to carry out has been dragging. The newspaper article was published in February. The Minister today in committee attempted to defend the potential for further delays by suggesting that perhaps this appointee might not hear tribunal hearings.
It seems to me that the Minister is not prepared to show leadership in this area, which has in fact been hailed around the world as an exemplary human rights process. The tribunal and the commission have been set in place. Over the last decade in Canada we have developed a forum for Canadians to bring forth grievances, whether they be in employment or with respect to sexual orientation. Of course, in the area of sexual orientation we certainly need further definition and clarification from the Minister. That process is now being threatened because the Minister has continually and repeatedly refused to set down a series of objective criteria for the appointment of officers and commissioners for the purpose of hearing complaints.
If the Minister does not act expeditiously in the case of Whyard, and if the Minister continues to shirk his responsibility as he did in the case of Arcangel, then, unfortunately, the whole human rights process in Canada will be undermined. As a result, what was in fact an exemplary system which was written about and exhibited throughout the world as a stellar example of human rights development will be destroyed. I think the responsibility for that destruction lies squarely on the shoulders of the Minister of Justice who has repeatedly shown that he is not interested in appointing quality members to the Human Rights Commission but, rather, is interested in using the tribunal as a resting place for old Tory hacks.

And what did we do? We said: "Our

appointments will be submitted afterwards to a committee of the House for a full public examination."
That is an initiative our government has taken, contrary to the Liberal government which did nothing for 20 years and practised shameless and excessive patronage. About Mr. Arcangel, Mr. Speaker, let me quote from a telegram he sent the Minister of Justice in November 1986:

-I am hereby withdrawing my name from the list of human rights tribunal panel because Ms. Sheila Copps unfair remarks and unjust allegations have seriously impaired my ability to serve effectively as a member of such a tribunal. And the telegram does not end there.
So I want to say, Mr. Speaker, that respect for human rights should start with the Hon. Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps). She should behave in such a way that the Canadian public understand that Members of Parliament should be the first and foremost to respect human rights. In this case, the Hon. Member has disregarded Mr. Arcangel's most fundamental rights. And today, almost eight months later, a big fuss is to be made of it.

subtopic: CANADA MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION-COMPLIANCE WITH RENT CONTROL REGULATIONS
CANADA MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION-COMPLIANCE WITH RENT CONTROL REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, you may not be aware of it, but there are more senior citizens in my constituency than there are in any other constituency in the country with the exception of Victoria, British Columbia. It is a very stable constituency, a very stable community. Usually, seniors live in their homes for years and years. Some of them go on until they reach the age of 90 or more but, inevitably, as you know, Mr. Speaker, they are forced to sell their homes eventually and to go into apartments.
Usually, Mr. Speaker, this happens when a spouse dies. The surviving spouse, often a widow, finds it very difficult to carry on in the family home. There are difficulties in doing the work that is needed around the house; there are difficulties in finding tradesmen to do the work. At the same time, of course,
Adjournment Debate
expenses are going up. Generally speaking, at that stage, the surviving senior moves into an apartment setting, where someone else looks after the home. It is also at this stage that our seniors can expect to be able to live on the income generated from the proceeds of the sale of the family home, and hopefully, if they are lucky, to have sufficient left over to enable them to live a little better life-style than had been experienced to that point.
All of that is true, Mr. Speaker, before one takes into account inflation-and we all know what happens when inflation hits.
There was a period of time when, for years, we experienced very modest inflation, and then we shot up to double-digit inflation. Of course, when inflation was in the double-digit category, interest rates also increased, so that at least the investments of seniors generated a little more income. But all of that has changed now, with falling interest rates. While falling interest rates are good for the economy, they are bad for the income of seniors. Today we have falling interest rates, with inflation continuing to rise, with the consequent increases in the cost of living: higher food, clothing, and shelter costs.
In my constituency, and in Metropolitan Toronto as a whole, and I expect across the country, rents have risen enormously in the last few years, reaching the stage where senior citizens, and tenants generally, live in fear of receiving the rent renewal notice announcing the inevitable rental increase.
For these people, rents have increased, while their income has either stayed the same, or perhaps even fallen off. Our seniors are finding that the increased cost of living is eating into the capital that they had hoped to retain to keep themselves self-sufficient during their lifetime.
As Hon. Members may be aware, in the Province of Ontario a number of years ago the provincial Government instituted rent controls and a rent review process, to try to control, in some modest manner at least, the impact of inflation on rents. Those controls are subject to a great deal of controversy. Some people contend that they make things worse rather than making them better. But, at the same time, Mr. Speaker, they were put in place to control rents for people who needed that control: seniors on fixed income, or whose incomes were falling.
It is hard enough for seniors living in apartments that are subject to rent review and control in times like this, but there are those who live in apartments that are not subject to such controls, specifically those owned by governments: apartments owned by municipal governments, and apartments owned by the federal Government through the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation.

speakeroldname: Mr. Claude Lanthier (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
subtopic: CANADA MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION-COMPLIANCE WITH RENT CONTROL REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to respond to the question raised by the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Redway) on March 27 and tonight.
The issue of affordable housing in Canada is one that has concerned my government ever since we took office almost three years ago.
Following a complete review of all national housing policies, new directions were established that have resulted in far more truly disadvantaged Canadians receiving assistance.
The Main Square Complex, the home for many seniors, disabled and others of modest income which we are talking about tonight, continues to receive our attention and assistance.
Residents of Main Square who will have to renew their leases between July 1987 and June 1988 will experience the lowest rent increase in several years, 6.2 per cent. This level is within both the spirit and intent of the Ontario provincial rental guidelines.
Many of the tenants of Main Square already receive assistance in the form of subsidies if their rent exceeds 25 per cent of their gross income. Should the additional monthly payment result in any tenant exceeding the 25 per cent ceiling, assistance will be made available.
The additional revenue from the rent increases in 1987/88 will allow for a level of maintenance adequate to ensure clean and pleasant surroundings for the tenants while keeping rents at a reasonable level.
Mr. Speaker, my government believes in social justice and in assisting those in need. Main Square is another tangible evidence of our commitment to help the truly disadvantaged, even if it means a small sacrifice on the part of those who can afford it.
May 19, 1987
